author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Marikana’s wounds still bleed 14 years after police massacre
content:
Fourteen years after police opened fire on striking mineworkers at Marikana, the massacre is remembered not only for the 34 men who were killed, but for their absence in the lives of their families.


For some, the memory is of a father who never came home. For others, it is the loss of a breadwinner, a brother or a son. And for those who were children when the killings happened, it is the experience of growing up with memories that have become increasingly distant, while the questions about justice remain.


At a commemoration marking 14 years since the massacre, the families, activists and academics reflected on what Marikana means more than a decade later – and on its place in South Africa’s longer history of protest, police violence and struggles for dignity.


For the Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (Seri), which has represented the families since 2012, the central question remains accountability. Seri secured payments for 35 of the 37 families whose loved ones were killed by police. Two families have received no compensation.


Seri’s executive director, Nomzamo Zondo said the compensation process itself reflected a deeper problem in how the state understood the loss suffered by the families. “Part of that is a narrative that what the state is interested in compensating is the income that the miners would have earned. They do not want to account for the husbands, brothers, sons and fathers that they took away from the families,” she said.


For Zondo, compensation alone cannot address the significance of Marikana. The state also needs to acknowledge that the massacre should never have happened, she argued: “That’s what a public holiday on the 16

th

 of August would mean. It would say: we are saying never, never again.”


She said this was particularly important given the continued use of force by police in managing protests. “We’ve seen that police continue to manage protests through the use of violence. They have continuously refused to accept that their role is to facilitate protests as a constitutional right.”


Zondo also pointed to the failure to implement recommendations made by the panel of experts on public order policing and the management of protests. The panel completed its work in 2018, but its recommendations remain largely unimplemented.


Squalid living conditions in the informal settlement, Nkaneng, in the shadow of Marikana platinum mine, a source of immense wealth for the owners in 2012, Lonmin. Archive photo by The Benchmarks Foundation


Another major concern, she said, was the failure of the National Prosecuting Authority to bring those responsible for the 16 August killings to court. “Every year, of course, when the anniversary comes, there is an explanation that work is being done,” Zondo said. “But now we are like one year short from 15 years since the massacre. We are just 12 years since the Commission finalised its report and recommended that the NPA must investigate and charge whoever is responsible.”


The question, she said, was whether there was “really an intention to hold anyone accountable for the deaths of the 16

th

 of August”.


For the families, however, the consequences of Marikana are not measured only by the progress of criminal investigations or compensation claims. They are lived in the absence of loved ones.


‘I still have that memory’


NowilI Nungu was 15 when her father, Jackson Lehopa, was killed at Marikana. Today, at 29, she remembers him through the ordinary moments of their life together: travelling to school on a bicycle, buying him a Coke and watching him repair the bicycle whenever it broke.


“I have so many memories with my dad,” Nungu said. She was the only girl among six children and had been living with her father in Rustenburg while her mother moved back to the Eastern Cape.


By the time of the massacre, Nungu had moved to the Eastern Cape with her mother. The family did not have electricity and relied on the radio for news. Her father normally called every day after returning from the koppie to tell them he was safe. But that day, he did not call.


Crosses erected at the koppie as a symbol of lives lost on 16 August 2012. Archive photo by Muzi Mzoyi


Sebolai Liau lost his father, the late Janefeke Raphael Liau, at Marikana. For him, the question of justice remains unresolved. “I think regarding the Marikana massacre, there is no justice. I don’t think it will ever be served, but for now it has not been, and there are no signs …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: As streets close to welcome Xi, Egypt seeks space for strategic aims during China visit
content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down in Cairo on Tuesday evening for a highly anticipated visit to Egypt, his first in a decade. 


Several major roads were closed across the capital in preparation for the visit, with images of Xi and President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and the flags of both nations adorning the streets, signalling the intention expressed by both presidents to expand cooperation. 


But three former officials who spoke to Mada Masr about the opportunities and challenges the visit brings stressed that as much as the aim is to develop the relationship with China, the challenge is for Egypt to maintain its own development priorities while navigating between Chinese and United States influence.


Coming amid intensifying competition among major powers that places greater pressure on Egypt’s

long-standing strategy of diversifying its partnerships

, the visit is set to test Cairo’s ability to preserve its strategic autonomy while deepening ties with China.


Xi’s visit comes against a rapidly shifting global and regional landscape, from intensifying rivalry between the US and China to a renewed flare up in the war between the US and Iran. 


The Chinese president is

 set to arrive

in Cairo after meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Kyrgyzstan during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.

 


His high-profile visit to Egypt this week comes with recent talks pointing to expanding partnerships and investments and as Cairo’s relationship with Beijing is also moving into more sensitive areas, with new cooperation in artificial intelligence on the table and as the two countries currently hold their second, large-scale joint air force exercise across several Egyptian airbases.


For Cairo, according to former Ambassador to China Ali al-Hefny and former Assistant Foreign Minister Mohamed Hegazy, the developing relationship with China should not be seen as coming at Washington’s expense. 


Deepening ties with Beijing offers Cairo another avenue to advance its development and national security priorities, they said, while maintaining its longstanding strategic relationship with other partners such as Washington. 


Can foreign investment and industrial cooperation translate into local gains? 


Officials have signalled that the visit should expand the existing portfolio of economic cooperation between China and Egypt. 


Hefny told Mada Masr that Egypt’s priority is not simply to attract investment, but to use the relationship to advance its own development agenda. 


Egypt, he said, is “obliged to carry on with our development schemes” while seeking to learn from China’s development experience.


Repeated high-level

exchanges

 between Cairo and Beijing over the past period, he noted, were aimed at ensuring the “continuity” and “sustainability” of bilateral cooperation and its “real development.”

 


In early August, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly expressed his commitment to expanding strategic cooperation with China, pointing to Chinese investments in Egypt surpassing

US$10 billion

, as he gathered senior Egyptian economic officials and executives from major Chinese companies operating in Egypt.


The Investment Ministry has also announced new export contracts with Chinese buyers worth

$168 million

, as China’s two-year zero-tariff initiative for African exports took effect in May 2026.

 


These developments sit alongside the major Chinese-backed infrastructure

projects

 that have manifested in the last decade, from the New Capital to the Suez Canal Economic Zone, including China’s support for Egypt’s entry into BRICS in 2024 and Egypt’s growing role as a gateway for Chinese companies to access other African and Middle Eastern markets.

 


The challenge for Egypt is to land investments that do more than create jobs or bring in foreign currency, with an emphasis on projects that build deeper capabilities within the local economy. 


“Our main goal in Egypt in this period is to localize industry,” said Hefny. “China has the possibility and the political will and is ready to help Egypt and our economy by co-producing in Egypt’s industrial sector to allow Egypt to produce more and make some of the foreign currency needed to import our necessities from the outside world.”

author: Nyambura Mundia
title: Faith and Fury: How Moral Populism Became Kenya’s Political Currency
content:
Religion has never been peripheral to Kenyan politics. Churches have provided welfare, organized communities and challenged governments; they have also offered political leaders networks of influence and a language of moral legitimacy. The relationship has never been straightforward. Religious authority has, at different moments, been used to reinforce political power and to confront it.


What deserves attention now is not the presence of faith in politics, but the changing relationship between religious authority and political legitimacy.


William Ruto did not introduce Christianity into Kenya’s political life. Nor did he invent the longstanding practice of politicians cultivating religious constituencies. What is distinctive about his presidency is the prominence of his own born-again identity within the exercise and symbolism of political office. His political biography is repeatedly narrated through faith, providence and renewal; his presidency has cultivated visible relationships with Christian leaders and institutions, particularly within evangelical and Pentecostal circles; and religious symbolism has increasingly accompanied the performance of presidential authority.


The question is not whether religion belongs in Kenyan public life. It plainly does. Nor is it whether Christians should bring their convictions into politics. They should. The harder question is what happens when religious authority moves beyond participation in political contestation and begins to furnish political power with an additional claim to legitimacy.


In Kenya, that question has acquired concrete form. Prayer has become part of the symbolism surrounding the presidency. Religious leaders have maintained close access to political power. Financial relationships between politicians and churches have raised questions about influence and patronage. And proposals to establish religious institutions within state spaces have raised a more fundamental question about the boundary between the faith of an officeholder and the institutional character of the state.


None of this makes Kenya a theocracy. Nor does it make Christian institutions a single political bloc. The church has never spoken with one voice, and religious actors have continued to challenge as well as support political authority.


But it does expose a tension at the heart of democratic politics: how can deeply held religious convictions shape public life without allowing any particular interpretation of those convictions to become the measure of political legitimacy?


That is the question this essay explores. Because moral populism does not require faith to enter politics. It requires moral authority to become political currency.


The sacramental logic of power


Political authority has rarely been purely secular. Rulers have long sought legitimacy not only through law, institutions and force, but also through claims about morality, tradition and the sacred. Christianity became embedded in the institutions and social structures through which colonial rule was organized, while postcolonial states across Africa have continued to negotiate the relationship between constitutional authority, religious institutions and public morality.


Kenya’s political history reflects this complexity. Churches have not simply been instruments of political power. They have been schools, welfare providers, mediators, and important sites of civic organization. They have also moved between proximity to political authority and resistance to it. During the authoritarian years, sections of the church worked alongside the state on questions of welfare and national cohesion, while others became increasingly critical of one-party rule. By the late 1980s and 1990s, clergy such as Anglican bishops David Gitari and Henry Okullu, Presbyterian minister Timothy Njoya and Catholic bishop Ndingi Mwana-a Nzeki were among the religious leaders using sermons, church networks, and public advocacy to challenge political repression and press for democratic reform. The National Council of Churches of Kenya also became an important institutional voice in the struggle for political and constitutional change.


That history matters because it complicates any simple account of religion and power. The church has not occupied a fixed political position in Kenya. Religious authority has at different moments been used to reinforce political order and to challenge it. The same pulpit that can lend moral weight to political …

author: Gerald Mirirai Mabweazara
title: Africa’s Assisted Reproductive Technology Boom Needs Public Governance, Not Just Private Investment
content:
Across Africa, assisted reproductive technology (ART) is expanding at an unprecedented pace. Fertility clinics are opening in countries where, until recently, couples had little choice but to travel abroad, often to Europe, India, or within the continent South Africa—to access in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and related treatments. The costs of travel alone made this a prohibitive option for the vast majority of Africans, before the costs of treatment itself were even considered. This transformation should consequently be welcomed. For many individuals and couples experiencing infertility, ART offers the possibility of parenthood closer to home, reducing the financial and emotional burden of reproductive treatment.


ART refers to a range of medical procedures used to achieve pregnancy through the manipulation of human eggs, sperm, embryos, or reproductive tissues, typically involving laboratory handling outside the body before transfer to the uterus. ART is primarily used to treat infertility when natural conception is difficult or impossible. Common ART procedures include:


In vitro fertilisation (IVF): Eggs are fertilised with sperm in a laboratory, and the resulting embryo(s) are transferred to the uterus.


Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI): A single sperm is injected directly into an egg to facilitate fertilisation, often used in cases of male-factor infertility.


Frozen embryo transfer (FET): Previously frozen embryos are thawed and transferred to the uterus.


Gamete and embryo donation: The use of donated sperm, eggs, or embryos when a person’s own gametes cannot be used.


Gestational surrogacy: An embryo created through IVF is carried by another woman (the surrogate) for the intended parent(s).


Much of this growth has been driven by African clinicians trained in Europe, North America, and South Africa who have returned to establish fertility centres in their home countries. Their entrepreneurial efforts are frequently supported by ongoing collaborations with international fertility specialists who provide technical expertise, training, equipment, and sometimes modest financial investment. These transnational partnerships have accelerated the diffusion of reproductive technologies across the continent and represent an important example of knowledge transfer benefiting African healthcare.


Yet this success story conceals a significant ethical and governance failure. While private investment has expanded access to fertility services, African governments have largely abdicated responsibility for both financing and regulating assisted reproduction. Fertility care has become almost exclusively the domain of private, for-profit providers, making treatment available primarily to those who can afford substantial out-of-pocket payments.  This contrasts with the broader healthcare system, in which essential or life-threatening conditions such as HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis are typically funded and delivered through the public sector.


The privatisation of fertility care therefore appears to reflect a selective pattern rather than a straightforward extension of how healthcare is generally organised in African settings. This marketisation is particularly troubling in a continent where infertility often carries devastating social consequences, especially for women living in strongly pronatalist societies characterised by persistent gender inequality. In many African communities, infertility is associated with stigma, marital instability, social exclusion, violence and economic insecurity. Despite these well-documented harms, fertility care remains largely absent from public health priorities.


The greater concern, however, is not simply the privatisation of fertility treatment. It is the privatisation of its governance.


In the absence of comprehensive legislation, fertility specialists are often left to determine their own standards of practice, ethical guidelines and operational procedures. Clinics effectively become their own regulators, developing internal policies regarding gamete donation, embryo storage, donor anonymity, consent procedures, surrogacy arrangements and parentage. While many clinicians undoubtedly strive to maintain high professional standards, self-regulation cannot substitute for state enacted laws and publicly accountable oversight. Regulation should not depend solely on the goodwill or professional judgment of individual practitioners.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies: A Community of Practice to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence
content:
Over the past year, Liberation Alliance Africa has sustained the

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Indigenous Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

. This Community of Practice is a collective of African feminist scholars, practitioners, organisers, artists, and movement builders committed to the dreaming and making of a world free from sexual violence through knowledge bridges.


Sexual violence continues to impact communities across the African continent, and class, ethnicity and religion play a critical role in making civilians in conflict-affected countries particularly more vulnerable. It disproportionately affects women and girls, and ethnic, gender and racialized minorities. Sexual violence is compounded by conflict, displacement, poverty, and gender inequality. It remains significantly under-reported due to stigma and under-prosecuted? Due to weak and corrupt justice systems. Sexual violence includes rape and sexual assault, sexual coercion and exploitation, including trafficking for sexual exploitation and conflict-related sexual violence such as using rape as a weapon of war. It affects people of any gender and age. 


Our starting premise is simple: sexual violence on the continent cannot be understood, let alone addressed, through frameworks that treat colonialism as history rather than a structural force that continues to shape theory, practice, and response to sexual violence. 


Coloniality was

coined

by Peruvian philosopher and sociologist Aníbal Quijano, and it describes the long-lasting pattern of power produced by colonial rule and shape

s

 how we approach epistemological frameworks through which violence is understood.

Epistemology deals with questions concerning the nature, scope, and sources of knowledge.

 A meaningful analysis of sexual violence must begin by seeking to decolonise knowledge and epistemic structures. This analysis requires us to interrogate the assumptions that underpin dominant theories, question whose expertise is legitimised, and create space for African feminist epistemologies to shape how violence is understood, prevented, and responded to. 


We felt an urgent need to organise as scholars and practitioners to generate new frameworks grounded in our histories, political realities, and lived experiences. Our analyses are rooted in our confrontation of the neo-colonial state, the global imperialist, extractive and patriarchal systems that shape our everyday existence. We arrive as feminists in service of a liberatory project, convinced that knowledge-making is itself a site of feminist struggle. 


As the CoP came together through both intentional convening and organic growth, we began organising our work around three enquiries that we believe are critical to envisioning a decolonial feminist approach to preventing and responding to sexual violence in Africa. 


The first enquiry,

Whose Knowledge? An Audit of the Current Knowledge Systems within Sexual Violence Prevention and Response in Africa

 examines the dominant literature, asks whose voices have shaped the field, whose knowledge has been marginalised, and what becomes possible when African feminist scholarship is placed at the centre of analysis. 


The second enquiry,

 The Coloniality of Sexual Violence: Gender, Power, Sovereignty, and the Neo-Colonial State,

 advances interventions on sexual violence that explicitly interrogate the role and impact of hetero-patriarchal colonial racial-capitalism, alongside the complicity of neo-colonial states, in producing and sustaining conditions of gendered violence. 


The third enquiry,

Truth-telling and Epistemic Sovereignty in the Prevention and Response Continuum

, centres on indigenous and endogenous knowledge systems as essential practice-based frameworks for reimagining prevention, response, healing, accountability, and collective safety.


The Imperative of Recentering African Epistemologies


At Liberation Alliance Africa, we believe African women and gender-expansive people’s knowledge-making and world-building are crucial to de-westernising normative assumptions and dominant approaches. African women and gender-expansive scholars must nurture new ways of knowing and being- knowledge that doesn’t just challenge dominant views, but creates a rich foundation for how we understand reality and tackle life’s critical questions.


For a long time, African women and gender minorities were treated as …

author: WoMin
title: On Language and the Pedagogy of Liberation
content:
Across Africa, colonialism was not only a project of economic exploitation and political domination; it was also a project of language and cultural control. Colonial rule sought to determine not only who governed and who had access to resources but also elevated European languages as symbols of intelligence and authority, while African languages were systematically marginalised. 


African literature captured this contradiction. In

So Long a Letter

, Mariama Bâ writes from within the tensions of expressing African women’s realities through a language inherited from colonial rule. Ama Ata Aidoo’s novel

Our Sister Killjoy

, similarly, exposes the uneasy relationship between English as a language of literary expression and also as a reminder of cultural displacement. These reflections continue to resonate with present-day realities across the continent, where language remains deeply entangled with questions of power, culture, identity, class, gender, and belonging.  


Today, access to education, legal systems, government services, and political participation in many African countries still depends heavily on competence in colonial languages such as English, French, or Portuguese.  


In Nigeria, for example, although more than 250 languages are spoken across the country, English remains the dominant language of governance, education or even policy discourse. Similar dynamics persist elsewhere on the continent. In Tanzania, although Kiswahili is the national language, many court judgments continue to be delivered in English. Citizens who do not understand English must depend on interpreters to comprehend legal decisions affecting their lives. 


For peasant and working-class women confronting mining, oil extraction, logging, large-scale agricultural investments, and other extractive projects, language exclusions carry profound consequences especially for rural women whose language is deeply tied to their relationship to land, water, forests, food systems, ancestry, and survival.  


Where information about government-proposed projects is often delivered in foreign languages without clarifying their implications including the terms of the proposed project, the risks it poses, the compensation being offered, or the legal mechanisms available to challenge it, their ability to give meaningful consent or organise resistance against it, then language becomes a question of power. 


Language in Women Learning Liberation and Translation as a Tool of Resistance

 


Language was central to the development of

Women Learning Liberation

  (WLL), WoMin’s 18-month political education course for frontline women activists. The first WLL cohort began in July 2024, bringing together 60 women from Cameroon, Guinea Conakry, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, South Africa, and Uganda. From the beginning, WLL understood political education not as the transfer of knowledge from experts to communities, but as a process of collective learning rooted in women’s own experiences and struggles. 


The Ugandan WLL cohort spoke eight languages and represented five different community struggles. English could provide a common language for some discussions, but relying exclusively on it would have risked excluding women from fully expressing their experiences, questions, analysis, and political imagination. WLL therefore deliberately incorporated interpretation into the political education process. Facilitation moved between English, Luganda, Runyoro, and Kinyarwanda, while participants themselves became active in ensuring that interpretation was taking place. 


As

Ugandan facilitator Sostine Namanya

 explained: “Language can work, but language needs to be budgeted for, language needs to be prepped for.” 


In many African contexts, people come from diverse language backgrounds and often speak multiple languages. While English or French may serve as common languages, reliance on colonial languages can reproduce unequal power relations and weaken movements. Interpretation and translation therefore become powerful tools for building multilingual and robust movements capable of deepening collective participation.  


In 2024, WoMin launched materials supporting the

Right To Say NO  campaign in East Africa

 in five languages, which join a plethora of knowledge materials and resources such as its award-winning film,

Women Hold up the Sky

 (2021) and a comic book,

Voices against Extractivism: Sheroes for Change

title: Sudan Nashra: Military strikes RSF convoy inside Chadian territory, sparks regional concerns | Kauda fighting pushes Otoro groups to demand Hilu’s removal from SPLM-N leadership | US proposes nationwide arms embargo on Sudan in Security Council
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

here

.


Washington is pushing in the United Nations Security Council to take the Darfur arms embargo nationwide.


US Senior Advisor on Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos put the proposal on the table on Monday, after first floating the idea at a council session in June. The draft would expand the 2005 Darfur sanctions regime to all of Sudan, while explicitly bringing drones and related technology under the embargo. The current regime expires in September unless amended or renewed.


Boulos pointed to the growing toll from drone warfare, saying drones accounted for nearly 80 percent of casualties this year and that both sides continue to strike civilians and civilian infrastructure.


Khartoum rejected the proposal outright. Sudan’s ambassador to the UN Al-Harith Idriss said applying the same restrictions nationwide would amount to equating “the state institutions and the rebel militia,” calling the proposal an attack on Sudan’s sovereignty.


Washington has to get past Russia and China, which both pushed back against expanding the sanctions regime and can veto any council resolution. So while the proposal has support from some council members, it is unlikely to go anywhere without a compromise.


Sudan’s drone war crossed its borders twice over the past days.


In western Sudan, military drones struck a convoy of hundreds of Rapid Support Forces vehicles on August 20 inside Chad’s eastern Ennedi region, near the Sudanese border. Two Sudanese military sources said the convoy had been assembled over several weeks at camps in southeastern Libya, and was preparing to enter Darfur through Chad using a new route through North Darfur’s Wadi Howar.


Chad condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty and warned that it reserved the right to respond, prompting the African Union to call for restraint and dialogue to prevent a regional escalation. The Sudanese military has yet to comment. 


On the other side of the country, the military said a strategic drone crossed into Blue Nile State from Ethiopian territory and was shot down over Dindro. 


Inside the RSF camp, its main ally in the war and its parallel government, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, continues to grapple with an internal crisis that is becoming harder to contain.


Fighting with one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, has returned to Kauda, the movement’s political and military center in South Kordofan, with control shifting between the two sides over the past two weeks.


RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo intervened and called for a ceasefire, but overlapping control on the ground made that impossible to sustain. The ceasefire collapsed, and Otoro fighters regained the upper hand in Kauda.


Some Otoro groups are now calling for Hilu to step down and are seeking alliances with other Nuba Mountains constituencies to challenge a political order that the SPLM-N has dominated for decades, but which has increasingly been concentrated in a narrow circle around Hilu, two Otoro leaders told Mada Masr.


And while there is still no end in sight to the war’s battles, Khartoum is preparing to use September’s UN General Assembly in New York to consolidate a post-Khartoum political posture and present its vision for Sudan’s political and institutional order after the war, according to Sudanese diplomatic and government sources informed of the preparations. 


Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan remains the leading option to head the delegation. But US sanctions imposed on him in 2025 could make his participation complicated, prompting the government to consider other senior officials if necessary.


The government plans to put its internal political dialogue on the New York agenda. The process, now being hurried in Khartoum, is to be presented as nationally owned, with international actors there to support and facilitate rather than dictate its agenda or outcome.


But a political source close to the dialogue said New York will test the international response to a process whose current, state-curated form is already being rejected by parts of the civilian political camp. 


Sudanese political and civilian forces, opposed to both the war and a military-led political process, rejected Burhan’s call for a dialogue, saying that any process launched while fighting continues — and conducted under military control — would reproduce …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Mamdani Unveils AI Moratorium for Schools Through 8th Grade, Screen Time Limits
content:
Officials say the moratorium is the most sweeping of its kind.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a one-year ban on the use of student-facing generative AI across the city’s public schools through eighth grade, and restrictions on the use of the technology in high schools.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way,” said Mamdani in a statement.

The moratorium, announced Wednesday, is a reportedly first-of-its kind policy that will be implemented for the largest school district in the country. It bars teachers from using AI for most tasks in the classroom, and bans elementary and middle school students from using the technology for school work. This represents roughly 600,000 students.

High school students can only use AI in limited instances, and the school district is launching a pilot program for specific AI tools for high school students to use. There will also be twice-yearly AI literacy courses that instruct students about the biases, limits, and ethical concerns related to artificial intelligence.

“Companion” chatbots, or ones that are made to develop relationships with the user, are banned across all grades under the new policy.

The school district will spend the length of the moratorium evaluating the program and making determinations over its efficacy. Community groups and city council members recently called for a two-year moratorium on the technology within schools.

“We know the purpose of AI companies whether they are making sports betting models or an education tool: it is to produce a profit. Here in our New York City public schools, our purpose is our students,” Mamdani said in a press conference.

The policy also sets screen time limits for younger students and recommends caps of less than an hour of screen time per day for elementary and middle school students, while students up until second grade won’t have access to individual screens at all.

Research has found that AI use is expanding rapidly across schools. The vast majority of high school and college students say they use AI to help with schoolwork, while a RAND Institute study found that more than 80 percent of students said teachers didn’t give them explicit instructions on how to use the technology.

Though AI use in schools has gone on relatively unabated by school districts and regulators, studies have found that a reliance on AI can have deleterious effects on students’ development. The Brookings Institute found in a recent study that its use in the classroom can “undermine children’s foundational development” and has already caused widespread damage across schools. Using AI as a shortcut for research, writing, and thinking does not allow children to develop key pathways for creativity, knowledge attainment, and critical thinking, the report warned.

New York officials said that the AI ban is the most comprehensive of its kind across the country, emphasizing the importance of such a policy for children’s development.

“We should never confuse a machine’s ability to produce an answer with a child’s ability to arrive at one. There is something sacred in the struggle to understand: the question asked twice, the page wrestled with, the mistake that becomes discovery, the teacher who sees possibility before a student sees it in themselves,” said New York state Sen. Robert Jackson (D) in a statement.

“That is where intellect is formed and independence begins,” Jackson went on. “In a democracy, we educate children not simply to know things, but to question, discern, imagine, and ultimately think for themselves.”

author: The Canadian Press
title: Removing a nod to Indigenous Peoples from Alberta birthday note “glitch” fixed: Smith
content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she stepped in to fix a “glitch” that saw Indigenous Peoples erased from her official statement marking the province’s 121st birthday.


Within an hour of sending the Alberta Day statement on Tuesday, the government sent an updated version removing the sentence including Indigenous Peoples from its English version.


Smith said public servants made the move and that she urged them to revert to the original statement.


“I said, ‘why don’t you just put up the original one? I thought it was fine, and so I’m not exactly sure what happened with that glitch,” she told reporters in Calgary at an unrelated announcement.


“We’re just excited to be able to celebrate Alberta Day and all of the various cultures, and diaspora communities, including Indigenous Peoples, who have helped to build the province,” she said.


“We want to celebrate everyone.”


Nevertheless, the change had already drawn concern from critics amid tense relations between Smith’s United Conservative Party government and Indigenous communities before the upcoming referendum on Alberta separation.


The vote on Oct. 19 is to ask Albertans whether they want to remain a part of Canada or begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separating from the country.


Treaty 8 Sovereign First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi called the removal of Indigenous Peoples from Smith’s statement deeply troubling.


“Our Nations are not a footnote to Alberta’s story,” he said in a news release.


He added it’s especially concerning as Smith’s government is advancing separation-related initiatives and challenging the constitutional status of treaty rights and the duty to consult.


“At a time when First Nations people are facing increased hostility for standing up for Treaty, the government should be affirming our place and history prior to Alberta’s story, not deleting it,” said Mercredi.


The rewrite also drew heat from the Opposition NDP’s Jodi Calahoo Stonehouse, who is a Cree and Mohawk member of the legislature.


“You might be able to erase us from your statement, but you will never erase us off our land,” she said on social media.


Yonathan Sumamo, spokesperson for government communications and public engagement, said in an email that Smith’s second statement was issued by mistake and that her first statement, including the government’s recognition of Indigenous Peoples, stands.


“We apologize for this error and any confusion that it may have caused.”


As of Tuesday afternoon, Smith’s statement, published on social media, did not recognize Indigenous Peoples. The government’s website was updated with her initial statement including Indigenous Peoples.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: City of Iqaluit recycling proposal sitting in limbo with Department of Finance
content:
Work to re-establish a beverage recycling program in Iqaluit seems to have stalled with the Nunavut government, after the city presented territorial officials with a feasibility study earlier this year.


Iqaluit residents lost the program in July 2025 after local business Northern Collectables discontinued the service. Iqaluit city council

passed a motion

 in December, asking administration to embark on a feasibility study for the municipality to take over the program.


The study analyzed adding a reverse vending machine and other container deposit options for the city, along with cost estimates.


The city then met with territorial officials, said city spokesperson Geoffrey Byrne, but can’t move forward without financial support.


“Council has been clear that any such program would need to be cost-neutral to the municipality,” he said in an email.


Nunatsiaq News asked the Finance Department what came of these talks but only received a statement from spokesperson Hala Duale that the department

“does not have plans to reintroduce a refundable container deposit program at this time.”


Derek Allerton, an Iqaluit resident who says he collected approximately 14,000 cans off the streets in the past year, said the Government of Nunavut’s response is frustrating.


“Tens of thousands of alcohol aluminum beverage cans litter the streets of Iqaluit, and millions of aluminum cans are going to landfill,” he said.


Some of these cans have made it to a fundraising bin managed by Aqsarniit middle school’s environmental club, which

started

 a beverage drop off this spring with help from the Department of Environment. But the club only accepts non-alcoholic beverage containers.


“In my personal experience, one in four cans littering the city are pop cans, and the rest are alcohol beverage cans,” Allerton said, adding the

 most popular brands he sees littering the streets are Molson Dry, Budweiser and Molson Canadian. 


The environmental club’s initiative is far from a solution, Allerton said. For many, it’s too far out of the way.


“There’s a lot of pop consumed in the city, so I think there could be easily multiple drop-off points for pop cans to be recycled,” Allerton said.


He added he was previously feeling hopeful 

about the prospects of the territorial government resolving the issue after Premier John Main wrote to him in June to assure him the city and territory were “actively working together” to resume a “successful long-term program.”


“The Government of Nunavut (GN) has received a proposal from the City of Iqaluit with several different program options and there is a group which has been meeting regularly to develop a city-led program,” Main wrote to Allerton in a letter dated June 22.


“As of today, there is no confirmed funding model or program structure, because the parties are still analyzing the different program options with their respective funding needs,” the premier wrote.


“We are committed to continuing our work with the city to develop a program with clearly defined roles and responsibilities.”


Main also shared with Allerton that the territory’s liquor commission is no longer collecting a waste management fee on alcoholic beverages until a “new solution” can be found.


Nunatsiaq News has reached out to the premier’s office to clarify his position on the funding of a new recycling program for the city but did not immediately hear back.


Nunavut’s Finance Department did not respond to follow up questions regarding whether it is committed to funding a program at some point in the future.

author: Kevin Carson
title: La Lagna della “Economia” che la Sinistra “Non Capisce”
content:
Di

Kevin Carson

. Originale:

On Larken Rose: The “Economics” the Left “Doesn’t Understand” Gets Dumber Every Day

, del 3 agosto 2026. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Se frequentate internet e siete di sinistra, vi sarà certamente capitato di essere deriso da qualche simpaticone di destra (magari con la testatina in nero e oro e #Bitcoin nel profilo) che vi dice: “voi non capite l’economia” o “ma andate a studiarvi l’economia!”. Quando, per qualche meccanismo perverso, tra le raccomandazioni di YouTube mi è comparso un podcast di Larken Rose (

Appreciating Capitalism

), ho deciso, data l’enorme stima dei suddetti simpaticoni per le sue nozioni di “economia”, di migliorare la mia conoscenza del soggetto.


È difficile dare un’idea di un suo podcast, o del suo livello di stupidità, visto che molte delle peculiarità stanno nel podcast stesso. Lo stile è Rush Limbaugh puro. La voce trasuda disprezzo. S’inventa un interlocutore di sinistra (“ignorante di economia”, ovviamente) facendo la vocina infantile, e risponde facendo la voce autorevole e spiegando quella che nella sua testa passa per “economia”, tutto quel genere di argomenti mediocri e prevedibili tipici di Thomas Sowell.


Inizia col classico cliché di destra: “non è capitalismo, è aziendalismo!” (o “capitalismo clientelare”):


Se non apprezzate il capitalismo è perché non sapete cos’è…


Molti di quelli che accusano il capitalismo parlano praticamente di aziendalismo delle grandi società che sfruttano la forza dello stato per ottenere favoritismi e arricchirsi e rubare risorse da altri paesi e tutto il resto. Questo, soprattutto nell’informazione tradizionale, è ciò che passa per capitalismo. Se siete contro, tutto bene, anch’io, perché lo stato che li favorisce significa costrizione.


E subito, senza sosta, passa a dire che dobbiamo ringraziare il “capitalismo” per quasi tutta la tecnologia che abbiamo.


Voi mi ascoltate perché esiste il capitalismo. Lo schermo che avete davanti esiste solo grazie al capitalismo. I cavi che lo collegano esistono solo perché esiste il capitalismo. E anche l’elettricità che passa nei cavi e tutto il resto, tutto quello che è in questa stanza, in questo palazzo.


E però alla base del modello di profitto aziendale che produce tutte quelle cose ci sono le connessioni con lo stato. Microelettronica, cibernetica e infrastrutture delle telecomunicazioni sono il prodotto delle ricerca finanziata dallo stato, soprattutto a fini militari, e dipendono fortemente dai brevetti; quello che Rose chiama “capitalismo clientelare”, insomma. Ma sono

anche

 esempi dei benefici del capitalismo. Che immagino sia come il gatto di Schrödinger. Sembra che il tipo non riesca a dire due frasi di seguito senza contraddirsi.


Il concetto di elettronica secondo Rose (che esiste grazie a un “capitalismo” che non comporta lo stato) non è lo stesso di chi ha qualche nozione di storia industriale. La cosa non si discute neanche. Il ruolo dello stato nello sviluppo dell’industria tecnologica è stato descritto bene da David Nobe in

America by Design

. Lo sviluppo della cibernetica, della microelettronica e di quella che sarà l’ossatura di internet sono frutto della ricerca del dipartimento della difesa.


Ad onor del vero, Rose condivide l’errore logico praticamente con tutti i polemisti di destra. Tutti dicono che le attività che fanno profitti grazie ad aiuti o protezionismi statali o grazie alla proprietà artificiale non sono “capitalismo reale”; dopodiché fanno dietrofront e celebrano come “

merito del capitalismo

” prodotti come l’iPhone, inventato da un’azienda il cui modello di profitto dipende dalla proprietà intellettuale, gli aiuti di stato e una politica estera neoliberale.


Rose non fa che ripetere tutto un miscuglio di argomenti della destra libertaria sull’imprescindibilità del capitalista. Se esiste la tecnologia complessa, o anche solo un’esistenza appena migliore di quella dei cavernicoli, spiega…


ecco che subito qualcuno il dito contro [fa la vocina di bambino arrabbiato] l’azienda miliardaria cattiva come il cattivo del film che inquina l’ambiente ed è prepotente e ingordo [fine della vocina], ma la realtà è che qualcuno ha qualcosa che tu non hai e può usarla per fare cose come questo computer, ad esempio, o il monitor o la videocamera che mi riprende. Come pensate che si possano fare queste cose o anche un microchip senza la megafabbrica che fa microchip per computer?


* * *

author: Lillian Kollross
title: Helpful or Hurtful? The Growing Privacy Debate Over Meta Glasses
content:
As AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, smart glasses have emerged as one of the newest technologies raising questions about privacy and consent. This week, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reportedly banned employees from wearing Meta smart glasses over privacy concerns.

Dubbed “pervert glasses,” Meta glasses are wearable computers, allowing users to take photos and videos, access artificial intelligence, and use other digital features without holding a phone. But unlike a traditional camera, smart glasses can make it difficult for others to know when they are being recorded.

Those concerns have become particularly apparent in incidents involving women. In California, a doctor was caught wearing Meta glasses while examining a female patient who had recently undergone a breast lift. In another incident, a TikToker used Meta glasses to film himself harassing comedian Diane Morgan while she was filming on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for her fictional documentary series Cunk on Earth.

Videos recorded with smart glasses have also become increasingly common on social media, including content in which users approach, flirt with, or harass strangers without their knowledge or consent. Instagram promised to crack down and remove these kinds of harmful videos, but no such action has been taken.

The backlash has extended beyond social media. Influencers who publicly post footage recorded with smart glasses have faced criticism and hate comments. When cyclist influencer Oliver Hooson posted a biking video filmed using Meta glasses, he lost dozens of followers and was called a “perv” in his comment section.

Even Meta’s high-profile celebrity partnerships have drawn attention to the controversy. Reality TV star Kylie Jenner recently partnered with Meta to promote a line of smart glasses, prompting criticism from users concerned about the technology’s potential for surveillance.

The British advocacy group Everyone Hates Elon went further, creating fake advertisements with an X-ray skeleton of Jenner with the slogan, “We’re Always Watching.” The same advocacy group also took shots at Meta with an ad that featured a photo of child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein wearing Meta glasses with the text “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.”

Courts and governments are beginning to respond as well. Last month, the New York State Court System banned smart glasses. A month later, England and Wales followed suit and also banned all smart glasses from their courts. In Germany, an advocacy group has also filed a criminal complaint against Meta related to the glasses.

This came after Meta filed a patent application for AI-powered facial recognition software for their smart glasses. The software would automatically capture people’s faces and convert them into biometric data without their consent.

At the same time, smart glasses have meaningful benefits that should not be overlooked. For those who are blind or visually impaired, the glasses help with reading, identifying objects, and accessing information from the internet. When users visit a new country or start a conversation with someone who speaks a different language, the glasses include a live translation feature.

While these features are beneficial to some, the perverts and creeps of the world are ruining it for the rest of us. As AI becomes a larger part of our daily lives, we must find a way to protect the privacy and safety of women and girls.

author: Alexandria Shaner
title: What the 1960s can teach us about cross-racial solidarity
content:
This article

What the 1960s can teach us about cross-racial solidarity

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


There is a particular kind of political amnesia that can overtake movements in difficult times. We remember the victories but forget the arguments that preceded them. We remember the marches but forget the years of patient organizing that made them possible. We remember solidarity as a feeling rather than a political practice.


Alice Echols’ “

Black Power, White Heat: From Solidarity Politics to Radical Chic

” is a useful antidote to that amnesia.


Echols tells the story of interracial and cross-racial organizing within the Black freedom movement through two organizations that bookend the decade: the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, or SNCC, and the Black Panther Party. The Panthers’ commitment to armed self-defense, and later debates over militancy and guerrilla warfare, form part of that history. Echols’ central concern — and the focus of this review — is the difficult work of solidarity: how movements build relationships across differences in race, power and political position.


This book arrives at an important moment. Across the United States and elsewhere, racism, xenophobia, and religious and white supremacist nationalism are again being mobilized to divide people who might otherwise have common interests. Authoritarian movements understand something the left sometimes forgets: people who can be persuaded to see one another as enemies are much easier to govern.


The question of how we build solidarity across difference is therefore an urgent question of power.


From Black Power to “Radical Chic”


The title captures the book’s historical arc.


Black Power meant, among other things, the assertion of Black autonomy, self-determination and political power.


White Heat comes from SNCC organizer Bob Moses’s metaphor for the transformative potential of white participation in the 1964 Mississippi Summer Project. Nearly 1,000 mostly white college students traveled to Mississippi that summer to support Black voter-registration efforts. Moses hoped their presence would expose white America to the reality of racial violence and help generate political transformation beyond Mississippi.


And then there was “Radical Chic,” Tom Wolfe’s infamous 1970 caricature of wealthy white liberals hosting a fundraiser for the Black Panther Party at Leonard and Felicia Bernstein’s Manhattan penthouse. Wolfe transformed cross-racial political solidarity into a punchline: wealthy liberals playing at revolution, fashionable people dabbling in radical causes. Echols argues that the essay became more than a satire of one awkward party: It helped create a durable political language for attacking solidarity itself.


What happened between those moments is the heart of the book. Echols resists a simple story of interracialism giving way to Black nationalism, or a morality tale in which one side was right and the other wrong. She describes experiments in solidarity that were sometimes extraordinarily productive, sometimes painful, and often both at once.


That complexity is precisely what makes this history useful now.


Solidarity is not sameness


The early SNCC experience illustrates both the promise and limitations of interracial organizing.


SNCC brought Black and white activists together in a shared struggle against segregation and disenfranchisement. But

Freedom Summer

 also intensified questions about power inside the movement. What did it mean for white people to participate in a movement led by Black people? Could interracialism reproduce the racial hierarchy it was supposed to challenge?


Echols gives this contradiction a particularly revealing form. Some Black SNCC organizers noticed that local Black people who had repeatedly ignored their appeals to get involved would suddenly listen to newly arrived white male volunteers. In other cases, white volunteers arrived in Mississippi with assumptions about how things should be done, even taking over office work that Black staff had been doing. The conflicts revealed a deeper problem: The racial hierarchy SNCC was trying to dismantle could reappear inside an interracial movement.

These questions shaped the organization’s strategy and eventually contributed to SNCC’s turn toward Black Power and the expulsion of white staff in 1966.

author: Valerie Anne
title: Everything You Need To Know About the Lesbians of ‘Silo’
content:
For the first two and a half seasons of the post-apocalyptic Apple TV epic Silo, we only had two lesbian characters, buried deep in the ground: a badass mechanic, Martha, played by Harriet Walter who rarely left her apartment, and her ex-wife Carla, head of Supply, played by Clare Perkins. Their relationship was not a major plotline, but I was happy for the representation anyway. Elder lesbians! The best at their respective jobs! Love to see it.

This season, we got introduced to some more lesbians, this time in the aboveground storyline. Congressman Daniel Keene finds out his younger sister Charlotte (Jessica Brown Findlay, who played queer on Harlots) had been in an accident while she was working as a Navy pilot. After she recovered, she joined her brother and the reporter Helen Drew (Jessica Henwick) to learn more about what brought her plane down, and there she met the Senator’s daughter Anna (Morven Christie). The two hit it off and were flirting on a private plane and I kind of thought that was the most we were going to get, but then the aboveground timeline had a little time jump and the next thing we know, Charlotte and Anna are married! They have a cute double-date night with Daniel and Helen and gosh you’d almost forget this was an apocalypse show.

However, at the end of the episode, Charlotte is nowhere to be found. Daniel tries to text her and gets a response that makes him suspicious she doesn’t have access to her own phone. I texted my friend, LESBIAN IN PERIL. Though based on how the episode ended…a lot more people than just Charlotte are in peril.

Now, for the majority of this season, I held onto a bonkers theory: I thought the aboveground and belowground timelines were running concurrently. I was so convinced the silos were a social experiment being done before any nukes had ever gone off. My theory was kiboshed by the end of the episode, HOWEVER, I still don’t think 300 years have passed between the aboveground timeline and what Juliette Nichols is up to. I think it’s possible it has only been 50 years, or fewer, and the Vitamin D+ they use to erase everyone’s memories, combined with the Pact and the “AI” voice, led them to believe it’s been a lot longer, telling them fictional stories about past rebellions and other resets. I think that’s why artifacts and relics were outlawed, lest they trigger memories. Otherwise, what would it matter if they had things from the old world? So now, my newest unhinged theory is: what if Charlotte IS Martha. This week, they talked about how the Vitamin D+ shakes memories up so bad some parents forgot to feed their own children. So it’s not unreasonable to think a person or two forgot their own name. And Navy pilot to mechanic isn’t an insane pipeline…JUST SAYING.

Anyway, I’ve been having a lot of fun trying to untangle the mysteries of this world, going full red string murderboard about it, and I am STRESSED but excited to see what Silo‘s season finale brings this week. Fingers crossed all lesbians will be found and accounted for, safe and sound and underground.

+ Comedian Amber Ruffin and her partner Kelsi Cleary-Hammarstedt proposed to each other at the same time (gay)

+ Lesbian baseball webseries-turned-TV-show Slo-Pitch is finally almost here: it releases on Crave on September 25th

author: Eden Fineday
title: Help us keep the syilx Okanagan beat strong
content:
At the bottom of kɬúsx̌nítkʷ (Okanagan Lake) in snpink’tn (Penticton) on Aug. 26, community members gather and pray for the health of the land and for those affected by wildfires this summer.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


This story was reprinted from our newsletter. Subscribe for updates

here

 and learn more about our Okanagan campaign

here

.


The Okanagan was the very first community IndigiNews committed to covering.


When we launched in 2020, we made a promise to report on syilx Okanagan communities week after week with a consistency that shows our care and respect for the peoples and their territories. 


For the past four years, that promise has been kept by our reporter in the region, Aaron Hemens.


Today, his work is at risk.


Aaron on the ground in April 2024, reporting on a cultural burn.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The funding that supported Aaron’s incredible reporting has ended. Without new support, IndigiNews will no longer be able to provide the same quality of dedicated storytelling we’ve offered in syilx Okanagan communities. 


Our goal

is to raise 

$35,000

 from our community of IndigiNews readers to keep Aaron covering the Okanagan. If we can reach our goal, we’ll be able to keep Aaron on the Okanagan beat for another full year — ensuring his vital reporting continues without interruption.


Keep the syilx Okanagan beat strong


We need to raise

$35,000

 to keep Aaron Hemens reporting from syilx Okanagan territory.


Help sustain independent, Indigenous-led local journalism.


Donate today


Aaron, a settler of mixed Filipino and European heritage, approaches his work with IndigiNews by centering the communities he’s reporting on. He believes journalism should be done in a good way — through building relationships that centre community protocol and accountability. 


As a man of colour, Aaron is very aware of what it means to be overlooked, misrepresented, and excluded in news media and beyond. This knowledge inspires him to show up at community gatherings, council meetings and court hearings to sensitively document the conversations that rarely make national headlines but nevertheless inform them.


nkwancinem Kim Montgomery dances at the Similkameen powwow arbour grounds on July 23, after being honoured for her 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance.

 Photo by Aaron Hemens


This trust wasn’t built overnight. It took years of showing up for the people of the Okanagan. 


Across “Canada,” local journalism is disappearing. News deserts are spreading, hitting Indigenous communities particularly hard. As a result, important decisions are going undocumented, local histories are getting left unwritten, and people are less and less able to hold powerful institutions accountable. 


Stories disappear and, with them, access to the beating hearts of entire communities. 


At IndigiNews, we believe all communities deserve reporters who know the people they serve — not only during moments of crisis.


That’s why

we’re asking for your help

.


Community members exit a canoe after arriving in Penticton on July 30. The canoe was carved by Herman Edward, who participated in the original journey in 2001.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


As a registered Canadian charity, every eligible donation receives a charitable tax receipt. Whether you become a dependable monthly

 Firekeeper

 or make a one-time gift, your support directly sustains independent Indigenous journalism.


Every dollar protects the relationships IndigiNews has created — relationships that cannot simply be replaced.


If you’ve ever read one of Aaron’s stories, shared our reporting, or believe Indigenous communities deserve devoted local journalism, please consider making a gift today.


Together, we can ensure the Okanagan continues to have the journalism it deserves.


$35,000 Goal


Donate

Help us keep the syilx Okanagan beat strong

 appeared first on

Indiginews

.
