author: rti_admin
title: India’s Unfinished Independence
content:
Every August 15, the flag goes up over the Red Fort, the anthem plays in every school and University for a day to celebrate being free. We call it Independence Day — the day India stopped being ruled by the British after two hundred years. And I celebrate it too. But every year, sitting with it a little longer than a headline or a holiday usually gets, one question won’t leave me. Free from what, exactly, and free for whom? The British extracted our wealth, silenced us, and treated us like subjects and inhumane instead of people. They eventually left. But did the thing they left behind actually go with them? Seventy-five-plus years later, many people are still living under a kind of threat, inhuman, and subject to no major change, and the political power is transferred from one hand to another. That time, foreign rule, and the present time, the elite and the oppressed class. caste, patriarchy, or social hierarchy systems- nobody ever really dismantled them, just handed them down like inheritance. The face in charge changed. For too many people, the situation underneath it didn’t. None of this is me rejecting the freedom we won or the people who died for it. It’s me refusing to let “freedom” become something we wave on a flagpole once a year without looking at who still doesn’t have it. After independence, many have hope for major change. We are ruling ourselves at least; nobody discriminates against us, but it is only theoretical, not practical.

We, the people of India, aren’t one religion. We’re not just Hindu, or just Muslim, or Christian, or Sikh — and the Constitution doesn’t lean on any of that in its opening line. It says: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” That’s a bigger sentence than it looks. India was never built to belong to one group. Many people are sacrificing their lives, their homes, their hope, their relatives, etc., every family, every tongue, every tradition, without asking anyone to give up who they are to be let in. The Constitution doesn’t just govern us. It protects the different ways we live, our culture, tradition, and language. But that raises a fair question: why does a free people need a document telling them how to live? If human beings are born free, shouldn’t that be enough on its own? For most of history, freedom on paper and freedom in real life were two completely different things. Before the Constitution, millions of people on this land weren’t fully recognized as human, and they were denied all human rights. No education, no right to object to injustice out loud, no fundamental rights. treated as animals; they were not counted as citizens. Two hundred years of British rule made all of that worse, and many people gave everything to end it. Even now, it’s worth asking: is that independence something everyone actually gets to feel, or is it still a promise some people are still waiting on? The Ambedkar Constitution is not just a rulebook. They wrote down a vision; it is a way of life, what Ambedkar called Prabuddha Bharat, an “Enlightened India” where every person could live with dignity and respect, no exceptions. A constitution isn’t a book or a scripture. It’s that imagination of a glorious society, made enforceable.

When Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the others wrote the Constitution, they weren’t just setting up a government. They were imagining a civilization. Ambedkar called it Prabuddha Bharat — an Enlightened India — where a person’s caste, gender, religion, or birth wouldn’t determine how freely they could move, speak, or live. Liberty, equality, and fraternity weren’t supposed to just sit in the preamble looking nice. They were supposed to be alive. On the eve of the Constitution’s adoption, Ambedkar warned that India was walking into a life full of contradictions — political equality on paper, and deep social and economic inequality in daily life. He said if that contradiction were allowed to go unaddressed, the people suffering under it would eventually blow up the whole structure of political democracy. That warning is still hanging over us, mostly ignored. Caste wasn’t invented by the British — it existed long before them, and it outlived them too. Dalits and Adivasis still face discrimination in villages, in workplaces, in schools, and even in death — separate cremation grounds, separate wells, and separate seating still exist in parts of this country. People still get attacked over things as small as riding a horse to their own wedding, wearing certain …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Not one surfaced despite court orders, families demand review of legal remedies
content:
Families of desaparecidos (enforced disappearance victims) and human rights defenders protest in front of the Supreme Court (SC) to push for the immediate review of writs of amparo and habeas data on August 28, 2026, on the eve of International Day of the Disappeared. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat

“Not a single success story, not one was recovered even with orders from the court.”

MANILA — Left with no choice but to push back, families of enforced disappearance victims called on the Supreme Court to review the writs of amparo and habeas data for “persistent ineffectiveness” for nearly two decades.

“Not a single success story, not one was recovered even with orders from the court,” Edith Burgos, mother of disappeared activist Jonas Burgos, told Bulatlat in an interview. She is the president of International Coalition Against Enforced Disappearance (ICAED) and vice chairperson of human rights group Karapatan.

Read: Bulatlat’s special archives on Jonas Burgos

The writ of amparo, which took effect in 2007, is supposed to protect an individual’s rights to life, liberty, and security against unlawful threats or violations. The writ of habeas data which took effect in 2008 is supposed to provide a remedy against unlawful gathering, collection, or storage of personal information and protects a person’s right to privacy.

“We wrote to the Chief Justice because there have been no positive results. We listed all the cases here and it is high time for the Supreme Court to review their own administrative order for the writs,” Cora Jazmines, wife of disappeared labor activist James Jazmines and one of the signatories of the letter sent to the SC, said in Filipino.

Read: A year after husband’s disappearance, Corazon finds more questions than answers

Since the writs took effect, human rights group Karapatan and Desaparecidos documented 272 cases of enforced disappearance: 206 cases in the administration of Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, 29 cases during Benigno Aquino III, 20 cases during Rodrigo Duterte’s administration, and Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has 17 cases as of this writing.

Prior to Arroyo’s administration, there were at least 2,000 unresolved cases of enforced disappearances.

“Rather than ensuring immediate protection and accountability, many petitions have been met with procedural delays, dismissals, or orders that are inadequately enforced. The persistence of disappearances across successive administrations—and the continued rise in cases even after the writ’s promulgation— exposes systemic failures in the implementation and enforcement of human rights protections,” Desaparecidos, a group of families and friends of victims, said in their letter.

Below are the following cases that the groups cited:

Karen Empeño, Sherlyn Cadapan, and Manuel Merino (Disappeared June 26, 2006, Hagonoy, Bulacan): The writ of amparo was filed on October 24, 2007, with the Supreme Court issuing the writ on October 25, 2007. Despite the Court of Appeals ordering their immediate release on September 17, 2008, the victims remain missing.

Romulas Robiños (Disappeared November 17, 2006, City of San Fernando, Pampanga): The Supreme Court issued a writ of amparo on November 8, 2007, but the Court of Appeals later dismissed the petition citing “lack of evidence.” He remains missing.

Nilo Arado and Maria Luisa Posa-Dominado (Disappeared April 12, 2007, Oton, Iloilo): A writ of amparo was granted by the Iloilo Regional Trial Court on December 17, 2007, ordering their release. They remain missing.

Jonas Burgos (Disappeared April 28, 2007, Quezon City): The writ of amparo was issued by the Supreme Court on December 24, 2007. The Court of Appeals partially granted the writ on July 17, 2008, ordering investigations. He remains missing.

James Balao (Disappeared September 17, 2008, La Trinidad, Benguet): The writ of amparo was partly issued on October 9, 2008, but later reversed on January 19, 2009. He remains missing.

Elizabeth “Loi” Magbanua (Disappeared May 3, 2022, Valenzuela City, Metro Manila): The Supreme Court issued the writ of amparo on August 23, 2022, and the Court of Appeals held the military accountable on September 9, 2022. Magbanua remains missing.

Maria Elena Pampoza and Elgene Mungcal (Disappeared July 3, 2022, Moncada, Tarlac): The writ of amparo was granted by the Supreme Court on November 29, 2022. They remain missing.

William Lariosa (Disappeared April 10, 2024, Quezon, Bukidnon): After dismissal of habeas corpus and amparo …

author: Alexis Vassiley
title: Labor’s Secret Harbour by-election loss is ominous
content:
Less than eighteen months ago, Western Australian Corrective Services Minister Paul Papalia comfortably held the seat of Secret Harbour, in Perth’s southern suburbs, with a two-party preferred vote of 61.5 percent in the state election. The by-election on Saturday wasn’t even close. One Nation currently leads 57-43 on a two-party preferred basis with 75 percent of the vote counted.

ON candidate Luke Herdegen’s 39 percent primary vote represents a swing of more than 30 percent to the party since last year. Labor’s primary vote plummeted to less than 25 percent, for a negative swing of 22 percent.

Labor’s campaign was utterly tone deaf. Papalia, who retired last month, triggering the by-election, told the

West Australian

days before the election: ‘‘We live in the best state in the best country on planet Earth, and part of the reason for that is good, solid, responsible government”. Anthony Albanese flew to Perth, not to campaign in the election, but for a $10,000-a-head fundraising dinner in a mansion on a street nicknamed “millionaire’s row”.

The party’s candidate selection was no better. Georgia Tree, a government relations advisor to Woodside Energy, was parachuted into what was considered “safe” territory. She previously worked for Federal Resources Minister Madeline King. Tree tried to leverage her working-class roots, saying how important Medicare and TAFE were to her parents. But all she could muster was a pathetic $100 fuel payment for motorists as her answer to the cost-of-living crisis.

Labor threw its all at the campaign, spending more than $400,000 (of which $14,850 came from Woodside). The premier seemingly never left the candidate’s side, while government MPs from all across Perth doorknocked. Labor also spent millions on a pork-barrelling spree and promised to finally start work on a train station they first promised ten years ago. But it was to no avail.

Despite what WA Labour tells itself, voters are not happy. A Demos poll in late August asked respondents if the state government was doing a good or bad job managing particular issues. Its

best

 result was 0 percent for “net good job” (i.e. the same percentage thought it was doing a good and bad job) for education and schools. On the cost-of-living, net good job was negative 56 percent; for housing it was negative 57 percent.

Indeed, the health and education systems are in crisis. The housing situation is thrown into stark relief on Memorial Drive, in the neighbouring Rockingham electorate, where hundreds of homeless people sleep in tents and caravans. Yet funding can be found to build housing for 1,200 defence personnel from the US and UK. In fact, Labor governments are spending billions of dollars on nearby military facilities at HMAS Stirling and the Henderson industrial precinct.

Secret Harbour is one of the least diverse seats in the state. There are fewer immigrants than the state average; those there hail largely from the UK, New Zealand and South Africa. Largely working class, more people have vocational qualifications than university degrees.

Gym owner Herdegen’s pitch centred on infrastructure, the cost of living, crime, immigration and housing. He told voters that Labor had neglected the area for too long, and this was an opportunity to send a message. Herdegen’s campaign did not shy away from far-right talking points. One social media video, for instance, talked about “saving the family suburb”, blaming a “population explosion” for ruining the “suburban Australian dream”, featuring white faces and nostalgic music. The One Nation campaign also spent a huge amount.

The Liberals did badly, coming third with around 17 percent of the primary vote (a negative swing of nearly 8 percent. State Liberal leader Basil Zempilas provoked a stoush with the Liberal federal MP for Canning, Andrew Hastie (whose seat overlaps with Secret Harbour), by claiming that a One Nation win would actually be a Liberal “victory”.

The Greens vote held mostly steady at 7.5 percent. The party campaigned on Labor’s neglect of the area, the cost of living, housing and against the AUKUS security pact.

So this was a good night for the racist far-right bigots of One Nation. The orange wave is real. Prior to Secret Harbour, it remained to be seen if One Nation could actually win seats off Labor. They can, and “safe” ones at that. Labor had held Secret Harbour and its previous incarnations since 1989. Only in 2008 and 2025 did Labor candidate need preferences to …

author: Mat Ward
title: The 10 most inspiring new protest albums right now
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for August.

Pro-Palestine protesters from Magan-djin/Brisbane rallied with activists from New South Wales' Northern Rivers at the Queensland border on August 1. They did so to highlight six words - "from the river to the sea" - that are legal in NSW but banned in Queensland. The same day, US protest singer David Rovics released his new album with Magan-djin-based musician - and long-time Green Left contributor - Kamala Emmanuel. It contains a song that, Rovics noted, is illegal in Queensland. On "From The River", they sing: "At the turn of the 20th century, it became a penitentiary, and at home or far away, you can hear them say, from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free." Two days later, British band Massive Attack were banned from Singapore for flying a Palestine flag on stage. Meanwhile, Rovics continued to release AI-generated protest albums as Ai Tsuno, his artificial intelligence alter ago. LISTEN>>>

On the same day Rovics released his latest Ai Tsuno album, the Socialist Alliance released a statement opposing the rapid expansion of AI data centres. A week later, the New York Times said a new Amazon data centre was stoking fears it "would be the most polluting power plant in the US". A fortnight after that, The Washington Post said Republicans had even started attacking Democrats for "being too soft on data centres". Addressing the data centre disgust is the new album from US punks The Carp, released on August 14. On its opening track, they yell: "They're going to put a data centre in your town! They're buying up the farmland in your town!" A week later, investigative journalists revealed the identities of the men behind viral, white, racist AI rapper Danny Bones. British-Jamaican rapper Lava La Rue noted “the irony of giving him a British-Jamaican rapping voice over a Black hip-hop beat". LISTEN>>>

Country-punk musicians Mike And The Molotovs liken people's fear of AI to the horror colonised people have been suffering for centuries at the hands of their invaders. On their new EP, released on August 15, they sing: "How will it feel to be colonised? When the robots come, they won't apologise. How will it feel to be swept away? We're going to find out some day." Just 10 days later, media outlet Quartz reported that US bank JPMorgan was expecting robot demand to surge. "At under $US10 per hour to operate, a humanoid robot undercuts the roughly $US30 hourly cost of a warehouse worker by a significant margin." Meanwhile, a new study estimated the earnings of people who are paying as little as $US10 a month to use music-generating AI platforms trained on humans' stolen work. Topping the list was remixer Cherry 葵 Nightcore, "bringing in an apparent $US2 million" from 941 million YouTube views. LISTEN>>>

Someone who already knows full well how it feels to be colonised, Indigenous rapper Miss Kaninna, released her radical new record on August 21. The groundbreaking Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung, Kalkadoon and Yirendali musician was raised by her mother Ruth Langford, who was recently hauled before court for taking part in an anti-logging protest, and grandmother Rosalind Langford, the co-founder of the Aboriginal Information Service, which became the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre. Discussing the album, Miss Kaninna noted she was about to play Mparntwe/Alice Springs, where "you have a complete fuckstorm of white people trying to control Aboriginal people's lives, right down to what we fucking put in our mouths". Two days before the LP's release, Mparntwe town camp resident Eileen Hoosan noted life expectancy became far longer when the Aboriginal community took control of health services from whites. LISTEN>>>

The life expectancy of Aboriginal people in Western Australia is 68.9 years. But the state government defines priority applicants for its Stolen Generations compensation payments as anyone over the age of 85. That means dozens of applicants who were taken from their parents as children are dying before they receive any compensation, The Australian reported on August 27. A fortnight earlier, West Australian Aboriginal rapper Kayps released his debut album, which rails against such injustices. author: Jerome Small
title: Vic premier’s attack on independent unions is an attack on decent unionism
content:
Organisations that offer workers some choice over who represents their industrial interests should be in the same legal category as violent fascist gangs and listed terrorist organisations. This is the intended effect of

amendments

 to laws governing incorporated associations, introduced into the Victorian parliament in mid-August by new Premier Ben Carroll’s Labor government. 

The law threatens to wipe out the Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU), which is a challenger to Labor’s largest affiliated union—the notoriously right-wing Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA). Much of the media coverage has presented Carroll’s appalling attack on RAFFWU as a straightforward factional payback, after the SDA-aligned faction within the Labor caucus supported Carroll when he rolled Jacinta Allen as premier of Victoria last month. 

Factional favours may well be a factor, but there’s more to it than that. 

As well as being a gift to the SDA leadership, Carroll’s move is part of a nationwide trend for Labor to crack down on any idea that workers should be entitled to seek representation from a union body not currently licensed by the state through the Fair Work Commission. 

Similar legislation

 to the current Victorian bill was passed in Queensland in 2022 under the Labor government of Annastacia Palaszczuk. And the

Australian Financial Review


reported

 in mid-August that Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth, a former SDA organiser, moved amendments to the national Labor platform at July’s national ALP conference “to bind the party to target ‘sham unions’”. According to the

AFR

: “The amendments say Labor will legislate to limit unregistered unions’ participation in industrial matters, including acting as bargaining representatives”.

Labor figures say that the main target of these moves are the so-called “Red” unions set up in recent years. These “Red” unions are indeed a crime against decent, principled unionism. Their main instigator is Graeme Haycroft, who has a long history in the Liberal National Party in Queensland and was a long-time, prominent member of the notorious 1980s union-busting think tank the

HR Nicholls Society

.

But the best remedy against right-wing unions preying on workers is political exposure, along with established unions demonstrating their superiority through organising strikes and industrial action that improve workers’ lives. This is clearly too much work to contemplate for most of today’s union leaders, and would run totally counter to their politics, which emphasises class collaboration rather than class combat. Much easier to just rely on Labor to wipe out any competitors through legal and bureaucratic methods.

It’s not just RAFFWU and the “Red” unions that are affected by Labor’s attacks. For a decade from 2015, the farm workers’ organising team of the United Workers Union conducted a series of effective—in fact,

outstanding

—organising drives among migrant workers on farms. These workers sometimes made use of the provisions in the Fair Work Act that allow workers to nominate independent bargaining agents to represent them at enterprise agreement negotiations. 

This enabled workers to get around the dictates of the Fair Work Commission, which enforces a legal monopoly on union coverage for most industries in Australia. In the case of farms, this state-sanctioned monopoly belonged to the Australian Workers Union, which had done zero organising on farms for decades and was utterly opposed to any other union doing this organising either. 

Removing the ability of workers to appoint an independent bargaining agent in these circumstances, which seems to be the intention of Rishworth’s proposed changes to national industrial laws, would pose a significant problem for workers in situations like this. Migrant farm workers would be able to secure decent representation only by overthrowing the entire national leadership of the AWU, one of the oldest and strongest bureaucratic machines within Australia’s union movement. 

There’s also the case of the

Independent Transport Union

, a breakaway from the Rail, Tram and Bus Union in Victoria. Unlike RAFFWU, the ITU didn’t start as a project of the left, but rather as a sectional breakaway representing train drivers. But regardless of its origins, the ITU has become an effective industrial force within V/Line, Victoria’s regional rail network. The ITU’s existence as an incorporated association is clearly …

author: Cecilia Judge
title: Victory for rank-and-file ticket in Victorian health union election
content:
A group of rank-and-file unionists have ousted the leadership of the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association (VAHPA) in a landslide election. The VAHPA Pulse ticket, made up of rank-and-file union activists, gained almost twice the vote of the incumbents, VAHPA Unity, and won all the positions.

The VAHPA Unity team has controlled the union for fourteen years and was backed by significant anonymous donations. By contrast, VAHPA Pulse, which I am part of, relied for our support on conviction and our reputations as experienced and uncompromising delegates and activists. Our victory is the culmination of many years of hard work and solid rank-and-file union activity.

The outgoing leadership took control of VAHPA with the ticket name “Clean Sweep”. Clean Sweep faced off against cronies of former national secretary Kathy Jackson, who was responsible for disgraceful corruption and whose actions gave bosses and anti-unionists ammunition to attack unions. Defeating them was an important victory.

However, after the new leadership stemmed the haemorrhaging of members and rebranded the union from HSU Branch 3 to the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association to signal the beginning of a new era, there has been little in terms of concrete improvements for allied health workers.

I started working in public health just a few months after Clean Sweep came into office. Coming from the community sector, I was excited at the prospect of better pay and conditions in the health system. Today, members are leaving public health for the community sector for the same reason.

However, it’s not just our pay and conditions that have gone backwards under Clean Sweep. Members have also become increasingly frustrated and angry with the lack of communication and transparency on the part of the leadership, as well as its hostility to rank-and-file activity.

After working on the front lines throughout the pandemic, allied health workers had an enterprise agreement pushed on us in 2022 that contained a pathetic 2 percent pay “rise”. As the cost-of-living crisis intensifies and the workload increases in quantity and complexity, VAHPA members increasingly find themselves unable to remain in the sector, whether for financial reasons or their own mental health, often both.

At the 2023 delegates conference there was hope that the situation facing allied health workers might start to turn around. A new public sector organising team presented its three-year plan to rebuild delegate structures and networks in the lead-up to our next round of bargaining. There seemed to be a willingness to involve members and an understanding of the central role delegates play in not only recruiting members but also helping them become active unionists.

We all left excited. Delegates formed new working groups. In particular, professional reference groups were established to provide a mechanism for different occupational groups within VAHPA to raise their particular issues within the union.  Given VAHPA represents around 50 different professions within the complex health system, this work was vital not only to assist the union organisers to understand the issues on the floor, but also to strengthen our identity and ultimately our industrial confidence. All this work was to help inform our strategy before negotiations began on our next agreement.

These exciting developments were unfortunately short lived. We were told by the union leadership, and directly by the secretary, that this work was undermining and divisive to the union as a whole. Radiation therapists, arguably our most organised profession within the union, had been taking initiative in organising across the state and reaching out to their interstate counterparts to learn from their industrial victories. This was attacked by the leadership, which accused these workers of leaving other professions behind.

The message was clear: the leadership calls the shots.

The 2025 delegate conference was very different. Even friendly attempts by members to connect with each other were responded to aggressively by the leadership. I was rudely shouted at by the secretary on the conference floor after I asked for clarification about staffing. Later, I was attacked by an organiser and a delegate (who ran for assistant secretary on the VAHPA Unity ticket) in front of other delegates when I, on behalf of a core group of rank-and-file delegates, offered to start up a rank-and-file WhatsApp chat to increase …

author: Susan Price
title: Songs of working class struggle:  Les Thomas brings ‘I Remember Everything’ home after British tour
content:
I caught up with Melbourne singer-songwriter Les Thomas, who is back in Australia after a highly successful British tour that took his music from London clubs and Oxford’s Blackwell’s bookshop to the Tolpuddle Martyrs Festival in Dorset.

Thomas travelled to Britain in July with a collection of songs about memory, working lives, history, love and resistance, unsure how they might connect with audiences on the other side of the world.

He needn't have worried. By the time he returned to Melbourne this month, he had performed across England, sold all of his CDs and found his songs had struck a chord in ways he had not anticipated.

Thomas told Green Left that audience members had approached him after shows to talk about their own lives and histories. “Some were moved to tears by the album’s title track, which travels across centuries of violence, struggle and resistance that underscores working class history,” he said.

One of the tour’s most unusual performances was at Blackwell’s Books in Oxford, where Thomas presented his new album I Remember Everything: Songs, Stories and Social History. The bookshop provided a fitting backdrop for songs about personal experiences woven into the fabric of history.

Then there was the Tolpuddle Martyrs Festival — a place where the struggle for workers’ rights changed history.

For Thomas, who has a deep connection with the trade union movement, performing at the festival carried particular significance.

“The Dorset village is synonymous with the six agricultural labourers who were transported to Australia in 1834 after forming a trade union and refusing to accept attempts to cut their wages,” he said.

Thomas performed four times during the festival weekend, from the Radical History school, multiple stages to an impromptu set in the festival bar that scored him an extra festival in North Devon.

The audience response was matched by strong reviews. Americana UK awarded the album four-and-a-half stars, describing it as “an absolute gem which should be studied line by line in schools”. Liverpool Sound and Vision gave it 8.5 out of 10, while Fatea Magazine described the record as “poignantly personal and deeply humanist”.

The album’s appeal is perhaps best explained by the breadth of its historical gaze.

The title song moves through the slave trade, palawa warrior Truganini, the Irish Famine, the Easter Uprising, King Leopold’s Congo, Guernica, Amritsar, the Tolpuddle Martyrs and the struggles of Appalachian mine workers. The vast sweep of history then gives way to personal memory within the much longer human story.

“The Last of the Old Holdens” looks at the disappearance of Australian car manufacturing through the eyes of those who lived through it. “The Life of Eloise” addresses violence against women and the responsibility of men to challenge it. “The Firing Line” confronts the destruction of civilian life in war and calls out the complicity of silence.

But I Remember Everything is not simply a political record. Songs about love, ageing, loss, family and the search for peace sit alongside the politics. Thomas’s insistence that individual lives matter — and that remembering them matters too — underpins the entire album.

Thomas wrote and produced the album, recording with Joshua Jones, Trevayne Fernandez, Justin Olsson, Craig Kelly, Ben Franz and Jason Bunn, with harmony vocals from Trudy Fatnowna Edgeley, Mandy Connell, Jacinta Percy, Kyana, Suzie So Blue and Emmy Ryan. Guus Hoevenaars predominantly mixed the album, with Carra mastering.

The album artwork also reflects Thomas’s preoccupation with history and memory.

Its cover features JMW Turner’s The Slave Ship, the 1840 painting created by the abolitionist artist in response to the Zong massacre, when enslaved Africans were thrown overboard from a British slave ship.

After taking these songs through Britain — and to a festival rooted in the history of the labour movement — Thomas is bringing them back to Melbourne, where they were written and recorded.

I Remember Everything will be released through Oily Rag Records on September 14. Thomas will launch the album with a rare full band celebration at the Northcote Social Club on Sunday September 20, joined by special guests Mandy Connell, Emmy Ryan and Suzie So Blue.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: How politicians and CEOs got addicted to profit
content:
Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

. By Quentin Beresford. NewSouth Publishing; 352 pages; $39.99

“Of all the prime ministers I’ve known, and I’ve known all of them since Menzies, Albanese is the most gambling-captured prime minister I’ve ever seen”, Tim Costello is quoted as saying in Quentin Beresford’s 2025 book

Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

.

Detailing the history of the gambling industry and its tight connection with the Australian political class,

Hooked

 provides the case for meaningful gambling reform, something neither major political party is willing to implement.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026, which passed parliament in August, hardly scratches the surface of an industry that includes sport betting, both at TABs and online, pokies, casinos and more.

Australian gambling losses are now at a staggering

$31.5 billion

 per year, and have been consistently rising since records began in the mid-1970s. The new legislation doesn’t ban advertising or inducements (like free bets or text messages). It doesn’t remove poker machines from our communities. And it leaves the casinos free to continue operating.

Despite being deemed “

the strongest ever gambling reforms”

 by Communications Minister Anika Wells’ office, the bill stops short of seriously impacting the companies making mega-profits. Beresford’s book gives insight into why, despite there being overwhelming popular support for gambling reform, both Labor and Liberal governments have never been willing to do it.

The entrance of the poker machine was a major turning point in the history of gambling in Australia. In New South Wales in 1956, pokies were legalised and rugby league clubs were given the sole right to operate them. These clubs, according to one expert quoted in

Hooked

, “‘subordinated their social agenda to economic interests’ and grew wealthy on the back of poker machines”.

These league clubs were often the centre of the community. In the 1960s, the South Sydney Junior Leagues Club had 45,000 members. It offered facilities and activities that were not always available to working-class people, like squash courts, a swimming pool, lounge and library. But it also had 111 poker machines, with more on order.

The profits that came from these poker machines in clubs all across New South Wales became the key source of income for the rugby clubs. Beresford quotes the CEO of South Sydney, who recalled that they became “fat, dumb and happy” on the profits from the machines. By the end of the 1960s, there were 20,000 poker machines across New South Wales. Today, more than

80,000 are operating across the state

. This is an increase in poker machines that is twice the rate of population increase.

The relationship between the sports codes and the gambling industry has continued apace. After the release of Labor MP Peta Murphy’s report “You Win Some, You Lose More” in 2023 following a Senate inquiry, the “heavyweights of free-to-air TV and the football codes went all-out to lobby the Albanese government to prevent an ad ban”. This is because it’s not just sports clubs that rely heavily on a revenue stream from pokies.

The AFL receives at least $30 million from gambling agencies revenue, and the NRL $50 million.


The NRL still has direct relationships with gambling agencies, with half the clubs sponsored by agencies. The revenue they receive is not taxed, as both institutions are not-for-profits. The free-to-air broadcasters get around

11 percent of their

 revenue from gambling ads. This amounts to $150 million from gambling advertising each year. These relationships mean that there are multiple institutions lobbying the government; the broadcasters, the clubs and the gambling companies themselves.

One chapter in Beresford’s book details the way these lobbying efforts helped to destroy attempts at reforming the industry by Andrew Wilkie, an independent MP from Tasmania. Wilkie had struck up an agreement with then-Prime Minister Julia Gillard, who was returned to power in a minority government with support from the Greens and independents. Wilkie’s main interest was the gambling industry, which had sucked huge amounts of money from Tasmanians via poker machines and the Wrest Point casino in Hobart. This was Australia’s first legal casino, approved by a Labor government in 1968 following a referendum.

Wilkie had previously campaigned against Coles …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Toronto students say One Nation is not welcome in Cessnock
content:
With less than 24-hours’ notice, more than 100 mostly young people organised a vibrant protest on August 28 to show Pauline Hanson and One Nation that they are not welcome in Toronto, NSW.

Toronto High students and Youth Rising (a group that supports Rising Tide) and others others lined the footpath at the Toronto Hotel where Hanson held a $1000-a-head fundraising dinner for One Nation’s Cessnock candidate.

Many decorated themselves as clowns. They created a festive atmosphere, dancing to rap and popular music including “9 to 5” by Dolly Parton, the Macarena and, of course, the Pauline Pantsdown hit “I don't like it”.

There were busts of chanting, including “Racist, sexist, anti-queer, Hanson you’re not welcome here”.

A number of those driving by showed their support, with excited waves, shouts, blowing kisses and vigorously honking their horns.

The NSW Police presence was mild, with occasional requests to ensure a clear passage along the footpath.

Two Toronto High students told me that this was their first protest, and that most people are their school mates. “We're so glad we came; we didn’t think it would make a difference but it did, we just feel so much better and we feel we can change things.”

author: anred
title: ¿La Libertad Avanza? Un balance marxista a casi tres años de la presidencia de Milei
content:
Javier Milei y Luis Caputo | Agencia Na


Para consolidar una hegemonía política duradera, cualquier gobierno necesita garantizar un ciclo de crecimiento económico de mediano plazo. A casi tres años de gestión de Javier Milei, el gran dilema radica justamente en la forma que asume ese crecimiento y las importantes dificultades que tiene el gobierno libertario para establecer un consenso social de largo plazo. La desaceleración de la inflación fue y es el objetivo central del gobierno, y fue avanzando hacia dicho objetivo a costa de un severo de ajuste fiscal, apertura comercial, tipo de cambio pisado, tasas de interés reales positivas y techos paritarios. Sin embargo, este esquema consolidó una economía dual: mientras sectores que ocupan poca mano de obra como el agro, la energía, la minería y las finanzas empujan un tenue crecimiento general, la economía orientada al mercado interno (aquella que ocupa gente) cae fuerte.

Por Cristian Caracoche.


El ajuste impactó de manera directa en el mundo del trabajo y licuó los salarios reales. Si tomamos los datos del INDEC, se observa una baja del 4% en el salario privado registrado y una pérdida del 17% en el sector público. No obstante, la caída sería mayor si se utilizara el IPC 2018 (que Milei descartó) para medir el verdadero costo de vida.


En relación a la ocupación, se destruyeron más de 300 mil puestos de trabajo privado registrado y cerraron más de 27 mil empresas privadas. La degradación laboral no solo empujó la tasa de asalariados informales al 37,9%, sino que disparó del 12,5% al 15,3% la suma de desocupados y subocupados demandantes.


En tanto que la burguesía (como clase) se muestra ganadora del mileismo (ya que obtiene cierta estabilidad para su acumulación a la par que el gobierno disciplina a la clase trabajadora), aparecen entre los heridos del modelo las fracciones mercado internistas del empresariado, lo que empieza a generar fisuras entre el capital. Frente a esto, la clase trabajadora no solo pierde salario y ocupación, sino que también caen fuerte las condiciones laborales.


Ante a esta situación, el escenario social presenta una llamativa parálisis de la protesta, registrándose un retroceso en los conflictos laborales y una baja sostenida en los piquetes. No obstante, este apaciguamiento no implica un consenso social ya cerrado, ya que aparece una resistencia pasiva que se procesa puertas adentro, y que se expresa en la sostenida tendencia a la baja del Índice de Confianza en el Gobierno (ICG).


Todo esto deja una gran incógnita a mediano plazo (la cual se empezará a develar en la elección presidencial de 2027): si la sociedad tolerará pasivamente esta transición histórica hacia una Argentina primarizada y con una fuerza de trabajo débil y precarizada, o si aquellas resistencias pondrán un límite a esta transición (y de poner ese límite, cual será la configuración resultante).

title: M.L. Berneri - Workers in Stalin’s Russia
content:
Author

: M.L. Berneri

Title

: Workers in Stalin’s Russia

Date

: 1944, Reprinted in January 1945

Notes

: This text version of the book was scanned and character recognized from the original print edition. It was lightly edited for clarity and readability, including standardizing dates of publications, capitalization, spelling, and punctuation that might be confusing. Original British spellings have been retained.

Source

: Scanned from original


Caption for illustration


 “In Our Country and in Theirs.” This is how the

Evening Gazette

 published in Moscow in its issue of November 14, 1936 compares the conditions of the workers in Capitalist countries and in the U.S.S.R. This cartoon is typical of the kind of propaganda put forward by the Soviet Government to convince the Russian people that they are a privileged nation, and that outside Russia only oppression and starvation exist.


Introduction


 It has always been difficult to know the truth about the conditions of life in Russia. Both the Communist and the Capitalist press have been interested in disguising the facts in order either to eulogise or to slander the “first socialist state in the world.” With the entry of Russia into the war the interests of communists and conservatives, labour men and reactionaries came to coincide. All the parties supporting the present Imperialist war realised that Russia could be an important factor in crushing Germany and, with a few exceptions, they set about boosting the regime and its leaders.


 Journalists who, till yesterday, had only referred to Stalin as the Red Butcher, Tory politicians who had thundered against the rape of Finland, trade-union officials who had denounced State dictatorship, military experts who revealed that Russian soldiers went barefooted, bishops who had lamented the immorality of Russian life and the murdering of priests, have now all joined hands to praise Russia as the greatest, mightiest, holiest of our Allies. Speeches are made, articles are written, pamphlets and books are published by the million to “sell” Russia to the British and American public. Such an advertising campaign does not take place to magnify the greatness of our American ally for example, but in the case of Russia our rulers and politicians have realized that it possesses still a great attraction amongst the masses as the “workers’ country.” By praising it they hope to get a more enthusiastic support for the war effort and increased production at cheap cost.


 The boosting of Russia remains purposely vague. We are told of the happiness of the Russian workers, of their high standard of living, of the superiority of their system of education but few details and fewer facts are attached to these assertions. Press and politicians have achieved the incomparable feat of talking almost incessantly about Russia while saying nothing about the regime or the conditions of life of the inhabitants.


 When the Russian-German pact was concluded the

Boersenblatt

, the daily news bulletin of the German book trade, published a list of anti-bolshevist publications withdrawn from sale on the orders of the Nazi authorities. Books on

Forced Labour in the Soviet Union, How the Russian Worker lives, Revelations about Moscow

, etc., could no longer be sold or bought.


 The “democracies” were no less tactful towards the Soviet Union when it joined the Allies. The Bookseller reported that most books critical to the Russian regime had been called back from circulation.

The Nation

, February 14, 1942, announced that: “Harper Brothers, which recently withdrew a biography of Stalin, has decided not to publish G.E.R. Gedye’s book on his experiences as

New York Times

 correspondent; and Doubleday, Doran will not issue the reminiscences of Alexander Barmine, former Soviet representative to Greece, who fled to this country after the Moscow trials. Both Barmine’s and Gedye’s books were completed, but the publishers felt that the times are unpropitious for books critical of Russia.”


 This is only one of the most obvious aspects of the suppression of information about Russia. Most information does not need to be suppressed by the publishers as it is never recorded on paper. The Soviet Government has a real terrorist organisation which employs every means to prevent information unfavourable to Russia from coming to light. Intimidation is used to gag men and women who have lived in the Soviet Union and who are prevented from speaking lest …

author: Tim Scott
title: Big Tech’s Debate Over “Open” and “Safe” AI Leaves Corporate Power Unquestioned
content:
Two seemingly contradictory letters emerging from the AI industry point toward the same future.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On July 24, 2026, an initial coalition of 25 technology companies and organizations, including NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Meta, released the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter, calling for wider adoption of AI models that institutions can download and modify. By August 3, more than 270 companies and organizations had signed, spanning Big Tech, venture capital, investment management, and the defense and security industries. Four days after Open Weights’ release, another letter, Pacing the Frontier, organized by employees of frontier AI companies with support from two AI-policy nonprofits, drew more than 1,300 signatures. It warned that leading companies may be close to automating AI research, accelerating development beyond society’s ability to understand or control the resulting AI systems.

The letters seem to argue for opposite futures. One presents wider access and fewer restrictions as the route to security and prosperity. The other asks the U.S. government to support an international effort to slow frontier development before competitive pressures make coordinated restraint impossible.

But they address different levels of the industry. Open Weights seeks to deepen AI’s already pervasive presence by making customizable models easier to embed throughout the economy and public life. Pacing the Frontier proposes government-backed management of frontier AI, the industry’s term for its most advanced and broadly capable models. That framework could make the small circle of companies building these systems indispensable to defining the dangers and writing the rules meant to restrain them.

Read together, the letters point toward a two-tier arrangement. AI becomes entrenched across society while ownership of its most powerful systems, infrastructure, and governance remains concentrated at the top. Their connection requires no secret agreement. It lies in what both take for granted: AI development will continue, public institutions will finance and adopt it, and private ownership and corporate power will remain intact.

The letters leave out harder questions: Who will own AI and decide its direction? How will it be used in surveillance and war, and how will it reshape work and deepen inequality? Whose lives and futures will be valued, and does the public have any right to limit or refuse a technology presented as inevitable? Beneath the language of openness and safety lie deeper a general agreement over corporate power, military dominance, elite rule, and the authoritarian currents shaping Silicon Valley’s vision of the future.

An AI model is the underlying system that generates answers, predictions, images, or other outputs. Its “weights” are the billions of numerical settings developed from patterns in training data. Releasing those weights allows organizations with computing power and expertise to download, run, and modify the model rather than use it only through a company-controlled service such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude.

Researchers can examine these models, test their weaknesses, and build specialized tools, while organizations can run them locally rather than send sensitive information to a commercial service. Yet proprietary, company-controlled services such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are not inherently safer: their operators can keep flaws from public scrutiny, monitor how people use them, impose restrictions, raise prices, or withdraw access.

But releasing a model’s weights does not by itself make the AI system open source. Under the Open Source Initiative’s definition, open-source AI must provide the necessary materials and the legal freedom to use, study, modify, and share the system for any purpose. Those materials include the model’s parameters, the complete code used to train and run it, and detailed information about its training data and methods. Most open-weight releases, by contrast, provide the finished numerical settings and enough supporting files to run or adapt the model, but not the complete training code or the required details about its training data and methods. The training data itself and much of the development process often remain proprietary or unavailable. Beyond the definition’s formal requirements, the labor arrangements …

author: Sanjiv Pandita
title: The Street Fighter, in Loving Memory of Apo Leong
content:
Editor’s Note:

 On Friday, 14 August 2026, Apo Leong, who had made enormous, decades-long contributions to Asia’s labour movement, passed away in Hong Kong.


Apo, who grew up in Macau and moved to Hong Kong as a teeanger, worked tirelessly as a labour reporter, organiser, campaigner and leader. He was a mentor and friend to a generation of labour activists in Hong Kong and across Asia.


For many years, Apo worked at the Hong Kong Christian Industrial Committee (HKCIC) with a focus on victims of industrial accidents, and led the Asia Monitor Resource Center (AMRC) as its first Asian Director until his retirement in 2008.


In his many roles over the decades, he built networks in Asia, developed collaborations with labour groups, and engaged deeply in initiatives strengthening grassroots movements on workplace health and safety. In his retirement, Apo continued to support the movement.


We spoke with Sanjiv Pandita, who had worked with Apo at AMRC since 2001 and succeeded Apo as AMRC’s executive director between 2008 and 2016. They collaborated closely on building the Asian Network for the Rights of Occupational and Environmental Victims (ANROEV) which unites workers across more than 16 countries to demand safe workplaces.


In this interview, Sanjiv shared his memories of Apo Leong as an dedicated activist, a mentor, a leader, and, in Apo’s own words, a street fighter.


Asian Labour Review (ALR): Thanks for doing this interview. We know you have known Apo Leong as a friend, colleague, and mentor for close to three decades, and worked closely with him. What are your first memories of Apo Leong?


Sanjiv Pandita (“Sanjiv”):

 The first time I met Apo was in Macau in 1999. I used to be based in Delhi, working on occupational health and safety. In 1999, I joined a conference in Macau. I met this really simple person. He was jovial and very welcoming, and that’s something that has stayed with me. Yet he was very forceful in how he structured his argument.


After the conference, we were having hotpot, and Apo was preparing the food for everyone. I said, “Hang on, I am not sure if this meat is cooked. He was laughing.” That was my first memory. Then we went out, and I saw a red Ferrari car. Apo said, “Oh, do you want to take a photo with that? I said, “Yes, why not? And Apo took out a camera and clicked a picture of me.


Then there was a job opening for a documentation officer at Asia Monitor Resource Center (AMRC), and I applied for it. I had an interview in Hong Kong and joined the organisation.


At that time, AMRC was located in a small flat, and every Thursday, we would have lunch in the office. After lunch, Apo got up and started cleaning the dishes. I thought, “Hang on, he’s the executive director of an organisation, and he’s cleaning the dishes?” That was not something I had seen in India. Apo came across as a very humble and down-to-earth person.


We would later observe another side of Apo. Apo would usually be very calm in meetings. But once he started talking about structural inequality and how we needed to fight it as a movement, you would see his passion. He looked like a very different person. That was his passion.


ALR: You worked with Apo for many years at AMRC. What was your day-to-day work with Apo like?


Sanjiv:

 On my first day in the office at AMRC, we went to a protest in the evening. Apo asked, “What are you doing? Let’s go! Let’s go! Let’s go! He did not tell us what was happening. This was Apo’s style. You had to guess. Then, suddenly, we were outside a hotel because there was union-busting happening there.


He would explain by doing things rather than telling you: this is what the Hong Kong movement looks like, and these are the people in the movement. He would take you to an action and introduce you to people in the movement. Apo would throw you into the water, and you would learn how to swim.


One of the characteristics of the AMRC, and much credit goes to Apo, is that it was very bottom-up and democratic. There was no hierarchy. The entire decision-making process was conducted through staff meetings. This was a highly collaborative process. He was not a director; he was a leader, but not a manager.


I remember in staff meetings, people could even shout at him. We could disagree and shout, and in the end, Apo was still my friend. There was no fear of Apo. We considered him to be our brother. He would look to what was good for a movement. He was not a good project manager. I believe …

author: Battlescarred
title: Gotman, Leah (1896-1978)
content:
A biography of Russian Jewish anarchist Leah Gotman, hounded by the Bolsheviks.

"the Bolsheviks are the worst enemies of the socialist revolution." Leah Gotman, at a Nabat meeting, 1920

‘Leah Gotman and Fanya Baron are two anarchist women of outstanding personality. In their teens they left Russia for America, where they were employed in factories and took active part in the labor movement. I knew the girls well, splendid specimens of independent womanhood, of attractive appearance, fine feeling, and strong mentality. At the first call of the February Revolution these two girls, together with scores of other Russian refugees, hurried to their native land. It was just such as they that had helped to make the October Revolution. Leah and Fanya felt their place to be in the midst of the proletariat, preferring particularly to work with the Southern muzhik, among the agricultural elements of the Ukraine, to whom they gave all the love and devotion of their rich natures. Subsequently both girls carried on cultural activities among the rebel peasantry led by their famous Bat’ka (“Little Father”) Nestor Makhno.’ Emma Goldman, Heroic Women of the Russian Revolution (1925)

‘Lea Gutman and Helena Ganshina were delegated by the Moscow Aid Society to travel North and distribute food, clothing and other necessaries among the politicals in the prisons and camps of Archangel Province. They went with the permission of the All-Russian G.P.U. (Tcheka). During their presence in the North, the Anarchists imprisoned in the Peretomansky camp declared a hunger strike, demanding better living conditions and transfer to Archangel. Because Gotman, Ganshina and Piot'r Skurikhin (an exile in Archangel fox 2 years) informed the comrades in Petrograd and Moscow about the Peretominsky hunger strike, they were arrested and sent to Moscow. Where the G.P.U. sentenced Gutman and Skurikhin to 2 years exile in Berezsov, in the Tobolsk Province. It required a hunger strike of seven days to change the sentence to exile to Narimski Kral, which is considered a more preferable place.’ Bulletin of the Joint Committee for the defense of revolutionists imprisoned in Russia, No 1. October 1923, Berlin.

Leah Isaakovna Gotman was born in Kovel, in the Volyn Governorate into a Jewish family. In the early 1900s, she emigrated to the United States, moving to Detroit, where she worked in a factory. In 1912 she married the anarchist Iosif Gotman (“Joseph the Emigrant”) and joined the movement. In 1917, she returned to Russia and engaged in anarchist activity in Odessa. In late 1918, the Gotmans took part in the founding conference of the Confederation of Anarchist Organizations (Nabat) and Leah was elected to the Nabat secretariat. In 1919, she and her husband joined the Makhnovist movement, where she worked in its cultural and educational department. under the pseudonym Elena Keller. During this period she was repeatedly arrested by the Bolshevik authorities in 1919–1920. After the agreement between the Makhnovists and the Soviet government, she travelled to Moscow, where she worked with Volin, who had also recently been released from prison. At this time, Iosif went missing, most likely murdered by the Cheka in the Millerovo district. Returning with Volin to Kharkiv, Leah was arrested on the night of November 26, 1920, and sent with Ivan Charin and other anarchists to Moscow, and then to Oryol prison.

Conditions in the Oryol prison were appalling, with no heating or electricity, and with damp running down the cell walls. Prisoners were kept in solitary confinement. The prisoners declared a hunger strike in protest, but it did not change their situation, and as a result of the hunger strike, Ivan had a mental breakdown.

The failure of the Bolsheviks to convict the Socialist Revolutionary leaders at a trial in early August 1922, meant that they did not want to repeat the same experience with anarchists. Therefore, they transferred the case to Ukraine. Thus, Leah Gotman, Charin and other anarchists were transferred to the prison at Nizhny Novgorod prison, then to Moscow, and finally to Kharkiv .On October 10, 1922, Leah Gotman, Alexei Olonetsky, and six other anarchists were released, whilst Charin and Aron Baron were sent into exile. Charin and Leah Gotman had struck up a relationship, and moved to Odessa for medical treatment.

The persecution of Charin continued. Following prison protests and hunger strikes, he was transferred to Arkhangelsk prison in April …

author: Samantha Agarwal
title: World’s Largest Far Right Paramilitary Rallied in NYC. It Should Alarm Everyone.
content:
Five thousand people attended a rally in New York City led by the right-wing Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On February 20, 1939, the Madison Square Garden arena in New York City hosted a chilling spectacle. A portrait of George Washington hung at the center of the arena, flanked by U.S. flags and swastikas. Over 20,000 people packed the stands to hear Fritz Kuhn, leader of the German American Bund — one of the most prominent U.S.-based organizations aligned with the Third Reich — project his vision of a “white, Gentile-ruled United States.” Outside, 100,000 anti-Nazi protesters clashed with police on Eighth Avenue, determined to stop the legitimization of European fascism on U.S. soil.

Eighty-seven years later, global leaders in ethno-fascism and their sympathizers returned to Madison Square Garden.

On August 29, 2026, 5,000 people gathered at Madison Square Garden to hear Mohan Bhagwat, the sarsanghchalak (Supreme Leader) of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). As the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the RSS is the world’s largest far right paramilitary organization, with an estimated 4 million members spread over 73,117 branches across India. Just as the Bund attempted to leverage the image of George Washington to legitimize Nazism in their rally of 1939, the RSS used this invite-only event — apparently attended by 180 religious leaders from 30 countries — to sanitize a century-old project of Hindu fascism. Obscuring its extremist agenda, the RSS cloaked the gathering in the rhetoric of liberal multiculturalism, branding it with the theme “Universal Oneness.”

In his 42-minute keynote, the septuagenarian Bhagwat played the part of a playful but discerning uncle, dispensing meandering aphorisms about an “innate, eternal oneness” that connects humanity and nature. Rooting these concepts in the Atman (soul) and India’s civilizational values, Bhagwat painted a picture of a nation that champions “unity in diversity.” In a jarring contrast to his movement’s actual record, he claimed that India chooses to tolerate its enemies rather than subjugate them — elevating the country as a global exemplar of enlightened governance.

While Bhagwat spoke inside, an interfaith and anti-caste coalition protested outside. It consisted of groups like SALAM (South Asian Left), Hindus for Human Rights, and the Indian American Muslim Council, along with members of some of the 66 organizations that signed on to a statement earlier this week condemning Bhagwat’s visit. Their speeches exposed the hypocrisy of Bhagwat’s claim to “unity in diversity,” demonstrating how the RSS and its massive network of Hindu supremacist partners — including nearly a thousand nonprofit organizations, cultural organizations, paramilitary groups, unions, and political parties, collectively known as the Sangh Parivar (or the Family of the Sangh) — routinely practice the exact opposite of what Bhagwat preaches.

Speakers pointed out how the RSS’s notion of unity is, in fact, exclusively reserved for Hindus — and only for those who are wealthy and upper-caste. Shree Baphna from SALAM talked about how Hindutva (or the Hindu supremacist movement) attempts to divert mass anger “away from those in power and towards those communities who are exploited and oppressed.”

When a Dalit [lower caste person] demands land, dignity and the annihilation of caste, Hindutva says, ‘forget caste – you are Hindu. When an Adivasi [Indigenous person] defends jal, jungle, zameen [water, forests and land] against mines, dams and corporations – Hindutva says, ‘forget your history – you are a vanvasi – a child of the Hindu nation.’ Shame!

Ritu Gupta from the nonprofit Hindus for Human Rights, noted that Mohan Bhagwat is here “pretending to spread the message of oneness.” But this is not the message Bhagwat’s supporters spread in India, Gupta retorted. “In India they say, ‘Hindus only – everybody else, get out!’ These Hindus who support the message of purging India of its minorities do not represent all Hindus. There could be no bigger hypocrisy than this!”

title: Памяти "Сократа"
content:
Сегодня мы вспоминаем нашего товарища Алексея "Сократа" Сутугу, он умер ровно 6 лет назад. Сократ был настоящим антифашистом, идейным бойцом. Его яркая харизма, желание всем помочь, всех защитить сделали его очень заметной фигурой в анархистском и антифашистском движении. За это его ненавидели власти и немало времени ему пришлось провести в неволе. Но даже этот опыт он сделал оружием в борьбе с властями. При всей своей известности в антифашистских кругах, у Алексея не было звёздной болезни. Он всегда оставался надёжным товарищем. Жизнь "Сократа" была такой яркой, что продолжает светить и новому поколению антифашистов.

author: Wolfgang
title: Verfassungsschutz-Klausel gefährdet gemeinnützige Organisationen
content:
Dossier


Es begann mit einer

grundsätzlichen Sache

: 36 NGOs kritisieren geplantes Steuergesetz 2013 / Offener Brief an Bundestagsabgeordnete

:

„

Zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen haben sich gegen ein Gesetzesvorhaben gewandt, das dem Verfassungsschutz ermöglichen würde, de facto über den Fortbestand gemeinnütziger Organisationen zu entscheiden. Sie forderten die Bundestagsabgeordneten jetzt in einem offenen Brief auf, dem Steuergesetz 2013, das morgen in erster Lesung im Parlament debattiert wird, ihre Zustimmung zu verweigern. Mit dem vorgelegten Gesetz will die Bundesregierung die Abgabenordnung (AO) so ändern, dass Organisationen, die in einem Verfassungsschutzbericht im Zusammenhang mit Extremismus genannt werden, die Gemeinnützigkeit ohne Prüfung entzogen wird (§ 51, Absatz 3, AO)

…“ (Presseerklärung vom 27.6.2012). Leider kamen schnell konkrete Fälle hinzu: dem Frauenverband

Courage e.V.

  und später auch

attac

 sowie

Doña Carmen e. V.

 wurde durch die jeweiligen Finanzämte die Gemeinnützigkeit abgesprochen, nun droht dies auch

VVN-BdA


 und

Campact,

  

DemoZ

  und

Change.org

 sowie

NachDenkSeiten

 und

innn.it e.V.

  und nun

Volksverpetzer

 – wir dokumentieren alle Aspekte der Problematik:


Grundsätzliches zur Gemeinnützigkeit


NRW-Landesregierung bekräftigt Recht auf politische Teilhabe gemeinnütziger Organisationen


„

Im April dieses Jahres stellte die AfD-Fraktion im nordrhein-westfälischen Landtag eine Große Anfrage zur „politischen Neutralität staatlich geförderter Organisationen“ (Drucksache MMD18-13444). Ziel war offensichtlich, gemeinnützige Organisationen – insbesondere solche, die sich für Vielfalt und gegen Rechtsextremismus einsetzen – durch das Infragestellen ihrer Gemeinnützigkeit politisch unter Druck zu setzen. In der Anfrage wurden konkrete Demonstrationen und teilnehmende Organisationen namentlich aufgeführt.


Die nun vorliegende Antwort des nordrhein-westfälischen Finanzministers (Drucksache 18-14721) ist eindeutig und unmissverständlich: Die Landesregierung teilt die Auffassung der AfD ausdrücklich nicht.

Stattdessen bekräftigt sie: Es gibt kein generelles Gebot politischer Neutralität für zivilgesellschaftliche, staatlich geförderte Organisationen – solange deren Aktivitäten im Rahmen ihrer satzungsgemäßen und gemeinnützigen Zwecke erfolgen. Gemeinnützige Organisationen dürfen sich politisch äußern, an Demonstrationen teilnehmen und aktiv an gesellschaftlichen Debatten mitwirken, sofern sie nicht parteipolitisch agieren.


Besonders deutlich wird dies in der Stellungnahme der Landesregierung:


– „Zivilgesellschaftliches Engagement im Zusammenschluss engagierter Bürgerinnen und Bürger, für ein friedliches, vielfältiges und respektvolles Zusammenleben, das auch menschen- und demokratiefeindliche Phänomene benennt und Extremismus sowie Radikalisierung entgegentritt, ist damit ein integraler Bestandteil der freiheitlichen demokratischen Grundordnung, der die Landesregierung uneingeschränkt verpflichtet ist.“ (S. 16)


–

„Während somit der Staat als Zuwendungsgeber selbstverständlich zur Neutralität verpflichtet ist, wäre es ein grundlegendes Missverständnis des freiheitlichen demokratischen Gemeinwesens anzunehmen, die der Sphäre der Zivilgesellschaft zuzuordnenden Zuwendungsempfängerinnen und -empfänger seien im Rahmen der Ausübung ihrer grundrechtlich geschützten Freiheiten ebenfalls zu politischer Neutralität verpflichtet.“ (S. 17)


Zudem stellt die Landesregierung klar, dass sie keine politischen Bewertungen zivilgesellschaftlicher Organisationen vornimmt und keine Informationen über deren politische Aktivitäten oder Ausrichtungen erhebt – weder im Rahmen von Förderentscheidungen noch darüber hinaus.


Antwort der Landesregierung: Drucksache 18-14721

 


Kurzbemerkung:


Eine erfreulich klare, überfällige und notwendige Antwort der NRW-Landesregierung: Es gibt kein Gebot politischer Neutralität für zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen. Diese Position sollten sich auch AfD, CDU/CSU – insbesondere Politiker wie Merz, Linnemann und Söder – endlich zu eigen machen. Denn es war nicht nur die AfD, die nach der Bundestagswahl 2021 mit einer Kleinen Anfrage (551 Fragen!) versuchte, zivilgesellschaftliche Akteure wie CORRECTIV, BUND oder Greenpeace ins Visier zu nehmen.


– Hintergrundbericht bei Legal Tribune Online (LTO):

https://t1p.de/kdzgw

 


 – Handreichung des Paritätischen Gesamtverbands zur politischen Betätigung gemeinnütziger Organisationen …

title: Der Server namens Paranoia: Verteidigt Autistici/Inventati vor dem 25.9.
content:
Seit fünfundzwanzig Jahren baut ein italienisches Hackerkollektiv eine Kommunikationsinfrastruktur auf, die Zensur, Überwachung und Polizeirazzien überstehen soll. Am 26. August stuften es die Vereinigten Staaten als terroristische Organisation ein. Am 25. September endet die Frist der Abwicklung.


Dieser Text ist eine Übersetzung von

«The Server Called Paranoia: Defend Autistici/Inventati Before September 25»

, vom 27. August 2026, von Sabot Media. Mit kurzem Kommentar und weiterführenden Ressourcen.


Es hätte eine dunkle und stürmische Nacht in einem italienischen Hacklab sein sollen.


Es war, ärgerlicherweise, ein schöner sonniger Sonntag.


Am 3. März 2001 versammelten sich rund zehn Personen im LOA Hacklab in Mailand um einen Computer, der aus ausrangierten Teilen zusammengebaut war. Eine Bank hatte ihnen einen alten Server zum symbolischen Preis von 15.000 Lire, etwa acht Dollar, verkauft. Sie bauten ihn mit ausgeschlachteten Komponenten, auch mit einer Festplatte von einem Heimcomputer, weiter aus. Niemand kam mit einem fertigen Bauplan. Softwarepakete wurden einzeln in Betracht gezogen. Jede Entscheidung wurde besprochen, bis alle einverstanden waren. Sie setzten bewusst die technisch am wenigsten erfahrene Person an die Tastatur. Der Prozess dauerte viel länger als nötig, weil Effizienz nicht das einzige Ziel war. Alle sollten verstehen, was sie bauten. An diesem Tag, erinnerte sich eine teilnehmende Person später, stellten sie fest: «A/I existiert jetzt.»


Sie nannten den Computer

Paranoia

. Im darauffolgenden Monat ging er online. Mit zwei Domains und zwei miteinander verflochtenen Geschichten: Autistici.org und Inventati.org. Fünfundzwanzig Jahre später, am 26. August 2026, stuften die Vereinigten Staaten Autistici/Inventati als Specially Designated Global Terrorist (ausgewiesene globale Terroreinheit) ein und setzten sie auf die Liste der Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (mit dieser SDN-Liste setzt die USA Sanktionen durch. Sie landet global in automatischen Screening-Listen und blockiert und erschwert Geschäfte).


Die Strecke zwischen diesen beiden Ereignissen – von einem recycelten Computer in einem Mailänder Hacklab zu den Mühlen des amerikanischen Sicherheitsstaates – ist die Geschichte eines Kollektivs, das ein Vierteljahrhundert damit verbrachte, auf einem gefährlichen Unterfangen zu beharren:


Personen sollten kommunizieren können, ohne sich zuvor Konzernen oder Regierungen zu unterwerfen.


Die unmittelbare Bedrohung hat jetzt ein Datum. Am 25. September läuft die Frist des US-Befehls aus. Institutionen müssen ihre Beziehungen zu A/I bis dann herunterfahren. Banken, Technologieunternehmen, Hosting-Anbieter und andere Institutionen werden angewiesen, verbleibende Beziehungen zu kappen. A/I baute seine Infrastruktur so, damit sie das Verschwinden eines Servers überlebt. Die Vereinigten Staaten versuchen nun, das Kollektiv wirtschaftlich und technologisch unberührbar zu machen.


Bleib dabei: Wir vertiefen, was A/I ist, zeichnen die Geschichte des autonomen Tech-Kollektivs nach und erkunden, was dieser neueste Angriff für Kollektiv und die breitere radikale Bewegung bedeuten könnte.


Vor A/I: Italiens Internet im Untergrund


Autistici/Inventati erschienen nicht aus dem Nichts. Seine Wurzeln liegen in mehr als einem Jahrzehnt italienischem autonomem Organizing, Piratenradio, Bulletin-Board-Systemen, besetzten sozialen Zentren, antikapitalistischen Bewegungen und Experimenten mit Computern als politischem Werkzeug. In den 1990er Jahren boten Netzwerke wie das European Counter Network und Isole nella Rete sozialen Bewegungen Online-Räume, als das Internet einem Grossteil der Öffentlichkeit noch unbekannt war. Italiens Hackmeetings brachten Programmierer*innen, Aktivist*innen, Künstler*innen und technologisch Neugierige in selbstverwalteten Räumen zusammen. Hacklabs ploppten in besetzten Sozialzentren auf, wo die Menschen Linux lernen, Netzwerke aufbauen und technisches Wissen als etwas anpacken konnten, das geteilt und nicht verkauft werden sollte. Die künftigen Mitglieder von A/I kamen aus verschiedenen Teilen dieser Welt. In Mailand verwendeten die mit dem LOA Hacklab verbundenen Personen den Namen

Autistici

, um ihre intensive Faszination für Technologie und ihren Wunsch, die darin verborgene Politik aufzudecken, zu beschreiben. In Florenz war das

Inventati

-Projekt mehr auf Kommunikation, Veröffentlichung und Bewegungsorganizing ausgerichtet. Zu den Projekten …

title: Rencontre avec Catherine Dorion sur Le courage et la joie. Comment traverser la tempête fasciste sans perdre le nord.
content:
Mercredi 9 septembre, Catherine Dorion discutera avec Sylvie Tissot au Monte en l'air de son nouveau livre Le courage et la joie. Comment traverser la tempête fasciste sans perdre le nord.


«

 

Nous ne sommes pas les animaux d'un zoo. Nous avons le choix. Nous ne sommes pas condamnés à la lâcheté. Notre énergie, notre cerveau, notre volonté, tout cela nous appartient. C'est le seul petit empire qui soit vraiment à nous, quand on y pense. Et il se trouve que ce petit empire est précisément ce dont les fascistes ont besoin pour chauffer leur enfer.

 

»


Alors que des personnalités autoritaires se hissent partout au pouvoir et que les discours de haine se multiplient, nous assistons impuissants à la montée de l'anxiété et nous nous y habituons. Nous vaquons à nos occupations. Car nous n'y pouvons rien, n'est-ce pas

 

? Pourquoi sommes-nous si désemparés

 

? Qu'est-ce que résister veut dire quand l'actualité nous dépasse, quand le pouvoir nous emporte dans son emballement

 

?


Pour répondre à ces questions, Catherine Dorion propose une chronique intimiste de l'année 2025, année de la rupture. Pour tenter d'y voir clair, elle l'entrelace de récits du passé qui témoignent de la vie quotidienne en d'autres temps où, comme aujourd'hui, la démocratie s'est fait prendre à la gorge par l'autoritarisme. Le courage et la joie cherche ainsi dans la vie réelle les amorces de la résistance, les failles par où passe encore et toujours la conscience humaine – et, donc, la lumière.

title: DHS Facial Recognition Software Used Against Minnesota 15
content:
Minneapolis, MN — Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) has deployed an aggressive facial recognition apparatus for monitoring and tracking domestic political dissidents, raising questions about why an agency created after 9/11 to fight the global war on terrorism is now maintaining centralized dossiers on ordinary American protesters.


Four days after federal agents

shot and killed Alex Pretti

 in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge, HSI began Operation Puppet Master, their undercover spying campaign that netted

conspiracy charges against 15 people

 who allegedly took part in protesting against ICE.


An HSI undercover agent, embedded inside the Signal group chat Whipple Watch, downloaded a selfie posted by Isaac Sant.


The photo shows Sant’s face bruised from rubber bullets. The agent uploaded the selfie to Clearview AI’s facial recognition database that turned it into a dossier.


Screenshot of a report titled DHS – ICE – HSI: Clearview AI Face Search Results prepared on Jan. 21, 2026 which features an image of MN15 defendant Isaac Sant.

 Page 1 of 8, document 212-29

 of the exhibits from a motion of discovery by Sant’s legal team.


“I was dismayed, but I wasn’t surprised,” Sant said. “HSI are a bunch of bozos and Keystone Cops that don’t know what the hell they’re doing.”


Kevin Riach, Sant’s attorney, revealed the breadth of the sprawling surveillance campaign, which targeted not the agents who shot and killed Alex Pretti, but protesters, union members, and activists who organized at churches, schools, and libraries.


Clearview AI

 boasts that its software can scrape over 30 billion images shared openly across various dead links and social media platforms, oftentimes without the consent of those photographed.


Riach said the government produced only a fraction of the Clearview AI facial recognition search results it generated on protesters and activists during

Operation Metro Surge

, arguing that all results should be disclosed.


“HSI employed Clearview AI as an investigative tool in this case,” Riach

wrote

. “The government has produced only two Clearview AI search results related to Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master.”


“It’s indicative of the type of sweeping dragnet surveillance that they’re putting the entire community under,” said Sant.


“This case involves an unprecedented campaign by DHS to spy on Minnesotans. During Operation Metro Surge, undercover agents posing as protesters surveilled community meetings at churches, parks, libraries, schools and union halls. These agents surreptitiously recorded dozens of conversations with ordinary people who were simply exercising their First Amendment right to protest ICE’s lawless rampage in our state. The agents gathered information about Minnesotans from law enforcement databases and internet searches, and created dossiers that are apparently now available agency-wide.”


Kevin Riach, attorney for MN15 defendant, in the his

motion for discovery

 submitted Aug. 13, 2026


Clearview, the New York-based facial recognition firm provides its database to thousands of local police departments and signed a

$3 million contract

 with DHS in the fall of 2025.


Clearview AI’s search results are far from perfect. A 50-year-old woman from Tennessee sat in jail for more than

three months

 after Clearview matched her image with a bank fraud suspect in Fargo.


“A woman used a fake military ID to steal tens of thousands of dollars from banks in Fargo. The cops ran surveillance footage through facial recognition software. That Al software said it was me,” Angela Lipps wrote on her

GoFundMe

 that has since raised $90,000. “A detective looked at my Tennessee driver’s license and my social media and agreed. Nobody called me. Nobody asked me a single question. They just got a warrant.”


Police arrested Randall Reid the day after Thanksgiving, accusing him of stealing designer hand bags in Louisiana. 


“I’m locked up for something I have no clue about,”

Reid told the New York Times.


Sant and his lawyer, Riach, said Clearview produced a false match in Sant’s case, linking Facebook photos of another man, his wife and their family to Sant.

„Alpha Gym“: Kollegahs Fitnessstudio wurde mit Graffiti bemalt
