title: Commemorations held for martyrs in five Istanbul districts
content:
Condolence gatherings and commemorations were held in the Istanbul districts of Esenyurt, Bağcılar, Fatih, Maltepe and Sultanbeyli for those who lost their lives at different times in the Kurdish freedom struggle.


The events, organised under the leadership of the Association for Assistance, Solidarity, Unity and Culture with Families Who Lost Their Relatives in the Cradle of Civilisations (MEBYA-DER), were attended by the families of the martyrs, representatives of political parties and many residents.


Esenyurt


A condolence gathering and commemoration for the martyrs was held in Istanbul’s Esenyurt district. Families of the martyrs, political party representatives and many residents attended the event at the Esenyurt district office of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party).


Chants of “Şehîd Namirin” (Martyrs never die) echoed through the hall, where photographs of the martyrs were displayed on a table decorated with flowers and candles, while photographs of Abdullah Öcalan were also hung in the venue. The programme began with a minute of silence, followed by speeches from the families, DEM Party Esenyurt District Co-Chair Serkan Yılmaz and DEM Party Istanbul Provincial Co-Chair Arife Çınar.


Yılmaz said that the martyrs had struggled for the Kurdish people’s language, culture and a free future, stressing the need to uphold the legacy they left behind.


Çınar called for their struggle to be continued. She also drew attention to the importance of the struggle to secure the political and legal status of the Kurdish people.


The speeches were followed by a video presentation about the martyrs and Abdullah Öcalan. The programme concluded with prayers and a mevlit, amid chants of “Bijî Serok Apo” (Long live President Apo (A.Öcalan)) and “Şehîd Namirin”.


Bağcılar


A condolence gathering was held at the DEM Party district office in Bağcılar, where photographs of the martyrs were displayed on tables draped in red, yellow and green cloth. Banners reading “Şehîd Namirin” and “Şehîdên me rûmeta me ne” (Our martyrs are our honour) were hung in the venue. The programme continued with a minute of silence and a video presentation.


The families said that the struggle of the martyrs had played an important role in enabling the Kurdish people to express their identity and speak their language today.


Free Women’s Movement (Tevgera Jinên Azad, TJA) activist Sebahat Tuncel said that the martyrs had left behind an important legacy in the struggle for freedom, democracy and peace, adding that upholding this legacy was the most meaningful way to honour them.


Fatih


At the condolence gathering in Fatih, photographs of the martyrs were displayed on tables decorated with red carnations and draped in red, yellow and green cloth. A video presentation was screened during the programme, while participants frequently chanted “Şehîd Namirin”.


Alaettin Altıntaş, who spoke on behalf of the MEBYA-DER, said that the martyrs had sacrificed themselves for a free and dignified life and that they would remain committed to the values they left behind. TJA activist Ayşe Aksoy said that they would continue to carry forward the cause of the martyrs.


A mevlit, a religious gathering featuring prayers and recitations, was held for the martyrs as part of the condolence gathering.


Maltepe


Banners reading “Şehîd Namirin”, “Têkoşîna Wan Rêya Me Ronî Dike” (Their struggle lights our way) and “Şehîdên Me Rûmeta Me Ne” were hung at the condolence gathering held at the Maltepe district office of the DEM Party.


 


The programme began with a minute of silence, followed by the singing of anthems. Participants chanted “Şehîd Namirin” and “Bijî Serok Apo”.


DEM Party Istanbul MP Özgül Saki offered her condolences to the families of the martyrs. The families received condolences following a video presentation.


Sultanbeyli


The commemoration in Sultanbeyli was held at the DEM Party district office. Banners reading “Şehîd Namirin”, “Têkoşîna Wan Rêya Me Ronî Dike” and “Em Şehîdên Azadiyê Bi Bîr Tînin” (We remember the martyrs of freedom) were displayed in the hall, alongside photographs of the martyrs, candles and carnations. Hundreds of people attended the programme, and some participants had to remain outside as the hall reached capacity.

author: Unknown
title: Gökalp: The commune is the key to living together - Part Two
content:
Suat Gökalp, who spent 33 years of his life in prison, began working to contribute to Abdullah Öcalan’s call for peace and a democratic society and his paradigm of communal society soon after regaining his freedom. Despite spending so many years under conditions of isolation, Gökalp speaks with a determination and clarity that leave little trace of the despair or anxiety often encountered outside prison. Drawing on his own life story, he spoke to ANF about conditions of isolation in prisons, the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the paradigm of communal society.


Part one of this feature can be read

here

.


There can be no communality without women


Gökalp continued: “Abdullah Öcalan says that social existence is itself communal. Communality forms the very core of socialisation. The first social unit, for example, was the clan, and there was a communal spirit within it. The clan family, which gave rise to society through communality, carried within it the nature of the commune. But with the emergence of the state and the patriarchal male mindset, that family structure began to deteriorate. Society comes into existence through communality. It creates and sustains itself on communal foundations: through collective life, collective production, collective consumption and the sharing of everything. And the founding force behind this is women. The history of women is the history of communality. There can be no communality without women. Through her reproductive capacity, woman ensures the continuation of the community. She cares for children, discovers how to gather plants and develops ways of securing a continuous supply of food, while also producing remedies from those plants. Woman keeps the hearth alive. There is, for example, the Mazda tradition in the Middle East. In Zoroastrianism, the Zend-Avesta evokes the idea of the hearth that never goes out. The hearth is a symbol representing an enduring strand of the communal spirit. Even curses have historically invoked the hearth. There is an expression, for example, meaning, ‘May God extinguish your hearth.’ In that sense, the hearth is a very ancient concept.”


History is the struggle between the commune and the state


Gökalp also said: “A women-centred social order and communality built around the mother did emerge. The departure from that social formation gradually gave rise to a patriarchal mindset based, at the time, on an alliance between the sorcerer, the military commander and the shaman, opening the path towards the formation of the state. This created a rupture, a division within society. Two paths emerged from this division. One sought to preserve society’s communal nature; the other was the path of the state. In Abdullah Öcalan’s paradigm, history is explained as the struggle between the commune and the state. Once the state and the commune diverged, this conflict continued to manifest itself in forms specific to different times and places, giving rise to the demand for less state and more society. That is our objective. Why do we say this? Why is this slogan important? Because the state expands by restricting the space of the commune. Öcalan’s paradigm does not reject the reality of class. But class alone is insufficient to explain the full extent of this rupture within society. Öcalan develops the analysis further. He argues, for example, that once communal nature began to deteriorate, the state sought to push back and weaken the communal sphere in order to expand its own, and that its first target was to restrict women’s sphere of life. We know this from mythology. In ancient mythologies, women are represented through the figure of the mother goddess and associated with life. But as the logic of the state begins to assert itself in Sumerian mythology, we suddenly see women associated with the underworld. The first contradiction therefore emerges as the state begins to target women. Once this division had taken place, both paths continued to manifest themselves in different forms according to time and place. We regard all struggles waged at different times and in different places around communal aims as socialist struggles. This is the heritage of socialism. We can trace this from the Qarmatians and the legacy represented by Jesus to the Persian Ismailis and Hassan-i Sabbah, from Hussein at Karbala to Kızılbash Alevism. In the West, it can be seen from the Dominican and Franciscan orders within Christianity to the Paris Communards and the …

author: Unknown
title: Najmeh Amini sentenced to 12 years in prison
content:
Pressure on activists and students from different communities who have taken part in protests in Iran continues. The Iranian regime continues to arrest students and activists on various charges and impose heavy sentences on them.


According to reports in student media, 23-year-old accounting student Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day in prison on charges of “engaging in operational activities against national security”.


Amini was detained on 11 February 2026 during security checks in the Ferdowsi Bazaar area of Mashhad, where she was subjected to violence by security forces, beaten and taken to Vakilabad Prison. She was held in solitary confinement in the prison’s security ward for around three months and is currently being held in a section known as “Aramesh”.


Denied access to a lawyer of her own choosing and the right to a fair trial, Amini was also accused of “insurrection”, “collaborating with Israel”, “insulting the leadership” and “clashing with a government official”. She was also reportedly pressured during interrogation to make a forced confession.


A case has also been filed against Amini at Branch 6 of the Criminal Court of Razavi Khorasan Province, with a hearing reportedly scheduled for the end of September.


Tabriz Revolutionary Court summons five Azerbaijani activists


A human rights organisation reported that, according to electronic notices issued through the SANA system, Sima Alipour, Hossein Esmaili, Vahid Abhari, Nima Radmanesh and Salar Taher Afshar have been ordered to appear for a hearing before Branch 3 of the Tabriz Revolutionary Court at the Shahid Beheshti Judicial Complex at 11:00 on 1 September 2026.


The five activists face charges of “propaganda against the regime”, “inciting public opinion” and “forging an official state document”.


One of those summoned, Salar Taher Afshar, is currently serving a five-year prison sentence in Evin Prison.


The summons issued to Sima Alipour comes at a time when women civil and political activists in Iran are facing judicial and security pressure as well as restrictions.


121 political and civil activists, academics and intellectuals issue appeal


Several days ago, 121 political and civil activists, academics and intellectuals from South Azerbaijan living outside Iran issued a joint statement expressing concern over the situation of Azerbaijani activists in Iran.


The signatories called on governments, United Nations (UN) special rapporteurs, the United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran and international human rights organisations to closely follow the situation of Azerbaijani activists in Iran and monitor the legal proceedings against them.


They also called for legal and diplomatic avenues to be used to guarantee the fundamental rights and freedoms of Azerbaijani activists in Iran.

author: Unknown
title: Tilbe Saran: Democratic principles will boost support for the process
content:
Actress and lecturer at the Department of Theatre at Kadir Has University Tilbe Saran, who was honoured with this year’s Honorary Award at the Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival, spoke to ANF about the relationship between peace and art.


Tilbe Saran reflected on how art can respond to prejudice, saying that rather than directly breaking down prejudices, art can challenge them by bringing people into contact with the experiences of others.


Saran said that theatre, cinema and literature are powerful mediums in this regard: “The reader or viewer does not simply read or listen to an idea; for a certain period of time, they enter another person’s world. I can say that one of the most effective methods in this respect is Augusto Boal’s Forum Theatre technique.”


Art holds up a mirror and can shorten the time needed to confront pain


Tilbe Saran also reflected on the relationship between art and confronting the past and said: “Prejudice towards a person or a situation often stems from seeing them as a ‘category’. Art, however, makes the individual behind that category visible. For example, when an identity such as ‘migrant’, ‘prisoner’, ‘elderly person’ or ‘disabled person’ becomes the story of a particular individual on stage, perceptions can change. Because we empathise. And, of course, art disrupts familiar ways of seeing. It can turn what we accept as ‘right’ on its head. On an issue where viewers consider themselves completely right, they may suddenly find themselves looking at it from the perspective of the ‘other’.


There is an important difference between providing information about an issue and allowing someone to experience it. Explaining that a prejudice is wrong is one thing; making the audience emotionally experience a confrontation with that prejudice is another. Emotional experience creates change.


Moreover, art creates this ‘simulation’ in a safe space. It can bring audiences face to face, in a controlled environment, with people and situations they might rarely encounter in real life. For this reason, theatre, cinema and literature can be seen as a kind of ‘social rehearsal space’. In this way, art at least makes prejudice itself visible. It holds up a mirror to the audience.”


Saran said that a certain distance is needed before some forms of pain can be spoken about, and that time can provide this distance. She said, “Art, however, can shorten that distance, that time.”


In women’s language, power becomes solidarity and negotiation


Tilbe Saran also reflected on the perspective of women who bear the heavy burden of an environment shaped by conflict and violence.


Saran said: “Women’s voices can make the unseen consequences of violence visible. War and conflict are often portrayed through armed confrontation on the battlefield. Yet women also face the consequences of displacement, increased care work, poverty, sexual violence, the breakdown of families and the disruption of everyday life, including something as basic as being able to put food on the table.


Women’s experiences can broaden the question ‘When will the war end?’ into ‘When will the social and human consequences of the war end?’ This can then redefine the concept of ‘security’. While the militarist approach reduces security to borders, the state, the military and weapons, women’s voices ask, ‘Can a person truly be safe if they are not safe in their own home, in their own body, in their neighbourhood and in their surroundings?’ This proposes a shift in perspective from ‘national security’ towards ‘human security’. It can also redefine ‘power’.


In a male-dominated world, power often means prevailing over others, exercising control and defeating the other side. In women’s language, however, power becomes the capacity to ‘act together’, to negotiate, to build solidarity and to bring about transformation.


In other words, it can bring the question ‘How will we live together?’ to the fore instead of ‘Who will win?’”


Peace requires justice, equality and coexistence


Tilbe Saran also reflected on the Peace and Democratic Society Process, arguing that the silencing of guns does not yet amount to “peace”. Saran also said: “The silencing of guns does not yet mean peace. Peace requires justice, equality, reparation, memory and the capacity to live together. Women’s experiences of life after conflict can make visible the fact that peace is a process that must be built in everyday life.


Language changes: it can change the way we …

author: Unknown
title: Kongra Star: Status of the Kurdish language is not negotiable
content:
People, women and civil society organisations in Rojava have mobilised against attempts to restrict Kurdish-language education in the curriculum. The people of the region and its communities stress that education in one’s mother tongue is a fundamental right and must never be sacrificed to political bargaining.


Kongra Star issued a written statement condemning policies aimed at restricting Kurdish-language education.


The statement stressed that the inclusion of Kurdish in the curriculum as a “national language” is an important step, but that limiting it to three or four hours a week or reducing it to an elective course is unacceptable under any circumstances.


Kongra Star recalled that the Kurdish people had endured years of denial and assimilation policies under the former regime, and that thousands of Kurds were stripped of their citizenship through the 1962 census in Hasakah (Hesekê), while their identity and culture were subjected to repression. Kongra Star said that the Rojava Revolution reversed this historical denial and that, since 2012, education in the mother tongue has become an integral part of everyday life.


Kongra Star also drew attention to the harmful impact such restrictions could have on children, saying: “Suddenly restricting the language of a child who has been educated in their own language for years to just a few hours a week could adversely affect the continuity of their education and their psychological sense of security.”


The organisation further stressed that women play a crucial role in preserving the mother tongue and passing it down from one generation to the next, and that restricting Kurdish also constitutes an intervention in the collective memory carried by women.


The statement underlined that the identity and language of the Kurdish people must be recognised if a democratic and pluralistic Syria is to be built, adding: “True integration does not mean abandoning identities; it means equal identities building a shared life together. Unity must be based on equality and the free will of peoples.”


Kongra Star set out its demands as follows: “Kurdish must have constitutional and official status as a language, unconditionally. Education in the mother tongue must be fully guaranteed in regions where Kurds live. Children must be able to study the entire curriculum in their mother tongue; this right cannot be made subject to political negotiations.”


The statement concluded with a call for all women to join the struggle, stressing that they would never relinquish their mother tongue or the gains they have achieved.

author: Unknown
title: Iranian forces arrest five Kurdish men in Marivan
content:
Iranian forces have arrested five Kurdish citizens from the village of Sardosh, Marivan, Kurdistan Province—Shirzad Abdi, Azad Norouzi, Zaniar Gaderi, Zaniar Tavana, and Pouya Kakeh Mohammadi—without warrants, transferring them to an undisclosed location.


The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that in the early hours of Saturday, August 29, dozens of security personnel with multiple vehicles raided the village of Sardosh in Marivan and detained the five citizens without presenting a judicial warrant.


Despite the families’ attempts to obtain information about their loved ones, the security and judicial authorities have refused to respond or provide any explanation regarding their situation.


No information is available regarding the reasons for the arrests or the charges brought against them.

author: David Venn
title: Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre’s new executive director prepares for opening day
content:
Annie Aningmiuq’s experience as an Inuk in the south is helping her imagine what might make future clients at Iqaluit’s Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre feel at home.


Take food, for example.


When Aningmiuq, the recently minted executive director of the healing centre, and her son lived down south, family members would bring her country food. If she went without it for a couple of weeks, her appetite for other foods would be lacking and she’d lose her energy.


At the same time, she said, if she ate maktaaq or tuktu by herself, it wouldn’t quite feel right. She needed her loved ones on the side.


“That aspect alone is magical,” she said in an interview about the power of making connections over a traditional meal.


That’s why regularly offering inuksiut, which roughly translates to “food for the soul,” to clients is one of the many plans that Aningmiuq says she looks forward to implementing when the healing centre opens.


There is still no clear timeline for when that will be. When construction on the $87-million centre began in August 2023, Nunavut’s Health Department said it

expected

 the building to be complete by December 2025.


“The last update we had was that it was going to be done by the end of this month and then they just came back saying they need more time but they didn’t have a specific date,” Aningmiuq said.


The healing centre is in the final stages of construction, said Chelsea Halvorson, spokesperson for the Department of Health, Friday in an email.


“Following substantial completion and final GN preparations, it will

transition

 to NTI and the Inuit-led not-for-profit who will determine when the facility is ready to welcome clients,” Halvorson said.


In the meantime, Aningmiuq is busy charting out programming, planning community visits, writing outreach materials and recruiting staff, which includes Inuit nurses and social workers who currently work in the south.


The availability of Inuit health staff shows some things are changing, Aningmiuq noted.


“When I was growing up, I didn’t know of one single Inuk nurse,” Aningmiuq said. “Now there’s multiple.”


Staff will have access to 25 housing units in a new complex downtown, she said, adding that “it’s going to open up a lot of opportunities for Inuit.”


Aqqusariaq translates to “a trail you go through to reach your destination.”


Located north of Toonik Pond, the healing centre will include facilities for both inpatient and outpatient care, including a daycare, traditional ceremony areas and two wings dedicated to trauma and addictions recovery, according to architectural firm Stantec’s website.


It will have a beading room, a sewing room, and an area for butchering, Aningmiuq said, adding there will be “elders-in-residence” as well as therapists, and an area for youth.


She said the centre will also have rooms with cribs so that, for example, if a mother wants to access Aqqusariaq’s services, she doesn’t have to leave her child behind.


“It’s very much Inuit-centred and focused when it comes to wellness and how Inuit need specific things that maybe aren’t offered in a southern institution,” Aningmiuq said.


Services will be available to Nunavut Inuit throughout the country, and Aningmiuq is looking forward to welcoming them.


“It’s going to take some time for people to want to take the step,” she said.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "We're Not Going Back": Ron Daniels on the Legacy of 1972 Gary Convention & 1963 March on Washington
content:
As Gary, Indiana, recovers from flooding and a two-week power outage, we also speak with Ron Daniels, president of the Institute of the Black World 21st Century, who discusses the city’s history as a site of Black struggle and organizing. In 1972, the city hosted the National Black Political Convention, which brought together thousands of activists to plan for increasing African American political power. Attendees included Coretta Scott King, Betty Shabazz, Jesse Jackson, Bobby Seale, Louis Farrakhan, Shirley Chisholm, Harry Belafonte and Amiri Baraka.


“It was one of the great gatherings in the history of Black people in this country,” says Daniels, who calls the current backlash to racial progress “the dying gasp of a system that needs a major overhaul.”

author: HATAHATA
title: Sanrizuka 40 years on: documentary on the Narita Airport struggle
content:
A 2006 documentary revisiting the Sanrizuka struggle forty years after the Japanese government decided to build Narita Airport. Focusing on the Toho district, where farmers continued to live and work under the flight path, the film documents the long conflict over land, development and state power. English subtitles have recently been added.

In 1966, the Japanese government decided to construct a new international airport at Sanrizuka in Narita, Chiba Prefecture. The decision was made without prior consultation with many local residents, including farmers whose homes and fields stood on the proposed airport site.

The resulting resistance developed into the Sanrizuka struggle, one of the most intense and long-running conflicts in postwar Japan. Farmers defending their land were joined by students and activists, while the state responded with compulsory acquisition, riot police and repeated attempts to complete the airport project.

This documentary was made around the fortieth anniversary of the original 1966 decision. It focuses particularly on the Toho district, where residents continued to refuse the sale of their land and to farm beside the airport. Aircraft pass directly over their homes and fields.

The film is valuable not only because it records the voices of farmers and long-time opponents of the airport, but also because it includes interviews with former airport officials, local politicians and supporters of airport development. This gives a complex picture of how the conflict continued decades after the most famous clashes of the 1960s and 1970s.

For readers familiar with libcom’s existing material on Sanrizuka, this documentary offers a later snapshot of the struggle and of the people who remained on the land.

English subtitles are available on the YouTube video:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1YhQFTq2JmM

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Left Behind and Overlooked": Indiana Energy Company Left Majority-Black Gary Powerless for Weeks
content:
Thousands of residents recently spent two weeks without power in Gary, Indiana, following a storm that ripped through the majority-Black city. The blackout ground the city to a halt, trapping residents in their apartments, forcing the closure of many businesses and leading to fuel shortages at gas stations. Officials in Indiana estimate the storm might have caused up to $5 billion in damage in Gary and other communities.


“We’re still in the recovery phase, as we speak,” says Gary Mayor Eddie Melton, who underscores that “hardening the infrastructure” should be a priority for the

NIPSCO

 utility company. “We’ve never seen wind this strong before. … They need to ensure that the utility grid system is going to sustain that type of wind.”

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: False drowning report triggers overnight search in Inukjuak
content:
A false report that a man had drowned in Inukjuak on Monday night triggered an overnight search while the community’s emergency services were already stretched to capacity, Mayor Bobby Epoo says.


A report that came in around 7:45 p.m. claimed a man had jumped into the river and drowned, he said.


The community launched a search-and-rescue operation, with a rescue boat deployed on the river and community members searching the coastline. It

 continued until about 1:30 a.m. Tuesday, Aug. 25, before resuming around 6 a.m., he said.


“On that specific night, the entire medical staff in the clinic and first responders were called in with other types of emergencies like accidents, pneumonia and conjugal violence,” Epoo said Friday in an interview.


A couple of hours into the morning search, community members told Epoo and municipal manager Aliva Tookalook that the alleged victim was spotted walking from where the incident had been reported. 


They later verified that the man was safe and called off the search, Epoo said.


In an Aug. 25 Facebook post, Epoo said that the village would pursue charges over the false report, citing the danger involved and the heavy drain on municipal emergency resources.


In an email to Nunatsiaq News, Nunavik Police Service public relations manager Julie Berthold said the initial information provided to first responders and to the municipality was “inaccurate and misleading.”


She said officers walked along the river and visited the alleged victim’s relatives and friends until he was found safe.


Epoo said one officer took a boat across the river to search the rocky and slippery shoreline, which posed a risk because the officer was wearing 70 pounds of equipment.


Four search-and-rescue members were on a boat. Others drove their personal boats, with two or three people in each.


There were also “maybe 20 other people” walking along the river’s edge and a licensed local drone operator, Epoo said.


Intentionally misleading police, including by making a false complaint to cause prejudice against someone, can lead to a charge of public mischief, Berthold said in the email.


Police are investigating, Berthold said, although no arrests have been made.

title: The Real Reason There's a Munitions Shortage? Too Many Wars & a Dysfunctional Pentagon: William Hartung
content:
Top U.S. military leaders have reportedly advised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against extending the war in Iran because ongoing operations in the Middle East have degraded the Pentagon’s ability to confront threats elsewhere. According to

The Washington Post

, the warnings appeared in a classified assessment for Hegseth prepared by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force and the four-star commanders overseeing U.S. operations throughout Europe, Asia and Latin America. This comes after multiple reports have revealed the U.S. is facing a critical munitions shortage, having used up much of its global stockpile of expensive missile systems during the war against Iran.


“The Pentagon is completely dysfunctional when it comes to fighting this kind of war,” says defense analyst William Hartung, principal adviser at the Project on Government Oversight. He says the U.S. policy establishment and the defense industry are less interested in effectiveness than in running a “money-making machine.”

title: Senado: el peronismo aprobó el blindaje judicial de Milei y votó a Yadarola, el juez de Lago Escondido
content:
Juliana Di Tullio, José Mayans y Wado de Pedro: todos votaron a favor del blindaje judicial de Milei.


Con los votos del peronismo, Milei avanzó en el Senado con la designación de 67 jueces. Entre ellos está Pablo Yadarola, uno de los magistrados del escandaloso viaje en avión privado a la estancia del magnate Joe Lewis en Lago Escondido, financiado por altos directivos del Grupo Clarín. Un aporte fundamental para el Gobierno en un fuero que tendrá bajo su órbita causas de corrupción que preocupan a Milei y a sus principales funcionarios. Entre los nombres de los votos a favor puede leerse a José Mayans, Wado de Pedro, Mariano Recalde, Juliana Di Tullio, Lucía Corpacci, Gerardo Zamora, Juan Manzur, Alicia Kirchner y Jorge Capitanich votando en común con Patricia Bullrich, Ezequiel Atauche, Luis Juez y Germán Abdala de La Libertad Avanza.

Por Juan Manuel Astiazarán (La Izquierda Diario).


El Senado aprobó este jueves 67 pliegos judiciales propuestos por el Poder Ejecutivo, en una sesión que dejó expuestos los acuerdos políticos que le permiten al Gobierno avanzar, en este caso, con el reordenamiento de la Justicia federal. 

Una complicidad abierta de parte de los bloques peronistas para el rediseño del Poder Judicial que pretende Milei.


Salvo el caso del juez Bertuzzi, que cosechó 23 votos en contra, 

el resto de los magistrados fueron designados por unanimidad.

 Esto incluye también el caso de 

Pablo Yadarola, uno de los jueces que viajó a la mansión del magnate británico Joe Lewis en Lago Escondido. El vuelo fue en un avión privado pagado por altos directivos del Grupo Clarín en octubre de 2022.

 La causa finalmente se terminó cerrando en diciembre de 2023 ya que se declaró nula la investigación, todo un símbolo de la impunidad con la que se manjea el Poder Judicial.


Yadarola se encontraba entre los protagonistas del escandaloso viaje a Lago Escondido, al igual que el actual ministro de Justicia Juan Bautista Mahiques (Foto: Lucía Giusiano para El Extremo Sur)


El peronismo, clave en el blindaje a Milei


Más allá de los fuegos cruzados discursivos, la bancada peronista terminó facilitando el avance de Javier Milei y sus aliados en el reacomodamiento de la justicia federal. Así entre los votos que designaron a los otros 66 jueces se pudo contabilizar unanimidad total, con 66 votos a favor y 6 ausencias. Libertarios, radicales y peronistas cerraron filas y aprobaron todos los pliegos, sin fisuras.


Entre los nombres de los votos a favor puede leerse a 

José Mayans, Wado de Pedro, Mariano Recalde, Juliana Di Tullio, Lucía Corpacci, Gerardo Zamora, Juan Manzur, Alicia Kirchner y Jorge Capitanich

 votando en común con 

Patricia Bullrich, Ezequiel Atauche, Luis Juez y Germán Abdala de La Libertad Avanza.


Uno por uno: el listado de los 66 votos a favor y las 6 ausencias que se registraron


La designación de Yadarola y Bertuzzi en la estratégica Cámara Federal porteña no es un dato menor. 

Este tribunal revisa expedientes de primera instancia sobre corrupción y otras causas que pueden involucrar al propio Gobierno

: desde el escándalo de la criptomoneda $LIBRA, pasando por la causa de presuntas coimas en la Agencia Nacional de Discapacidad, hasta investigaciones por enriquecimiento ilícito.


Yadarola es muy cercano al ministro de Justicia Mahiques y juntos fueron parte del viaje a la mansión del magnate Joe Lewis en Lago Escondido en 2022. Un símbolo de la connivencia entre jueces, funcionarios y empresarios que quedó expuesto en fotografías y numerosos chats expuestos en donde analizaban distintas estrategias para reducir los daños del escándalo. A pesar de eso, logró el acompañamiento de toda la bancada peronista.


Bertuzzi, por su parte, llegó a la Cámara Federal en 2018 gracias a un traslado irregular impulsado por Macri, apuntado por ser parte del lawfare contra Cristina Kirchner. Este último fue el único caso en donde se registraron 23 votos en contra por parte del peronismo.


Con este paquete, el Gobierno de Milei ya suma casi 180 cargos judiciales en menos de seis meses de gestión, 

una cifra récord que le permite avanzar en el control del Poder Judicial

, pieza clave para su proyecto de ajuste y ataques a derechos populares.


Mientras algunos referentes del peronismo intentaron despegarse con críticas verbales, en los hechos su voto fue decisivo. No es la primera vez: la bancada opositora ya aportó votos para el ajuste, para leyes de recorte y para que Milei avance con el PRO, la UCR y …

title: Podcast: Militarism and the Art of Slander
content:
By Marc Eliot Stein, World BEYOND War, August 31, 2026


From Seattle Opera’s “Barber of Seville”: David Gould and Roger Howell as Don Basilio and Don Bartolo


The following is a complete transcript of episode 87 of the World BEYOND War podcast. NOTE: Our monthly podcast usually features interviews, which we don’t transcribe since automatic transcription might not accurately reflect what our guests say. This month’s podcast is my own personal statement, a reflection of various topics ranging from the revolutionary legacy of classic opera to the histories of Haiti, Venezuela and Cuba to USA apartheid and USA’s war with Iran, concluding with a message about what it feels like for a middle-class urban progressive to be constantly accused of being privileged and out of touch.


Disclaimer #1: As always, this podcast contains only my own words and opinions.


Disclaimer #2: It’s unfortunate that I claim in this episode to have gained some ability to speak Italian and French by singing opera, because upon listening back to this recording I realize I badly mangled many Italian and French names here. I do think I am able to achieve some level of good pronunciation when slowly singing rehearsed parts, but my accuracy obviously drops once I get on a roll and start talking fast in English. Apologies!


Militarism and the Art of Slander


Welcome to episode 87 of the World BEYOND War podcast. I’m Marc Eliot Stein, technology director of World Beyond War, speaking from the Lanape lands of Brooklyn, New York. It’s August 2026 and the first thing I want to do today is express our love for the people of Nepal and China and Tibet, as we all try to grasp the enormity of the tragedy from the mudslide that began with a glacial collapse. This seems to be a disaster caused by climate change, and the world better wake the hell up because our planet is at a boiling point right now in more ways than one. Last month’s episode was about Asia, and our hearts go out to the people of Tibet and Nepal. 


I’ve got a lot to talk about today and I hope you don’t mind if I seem to ramble from one topic to another, because I actually do have a particular plan and purpose here today, and I hope it will all come together in the end.


I mentioned a few times on this podcast that when I’m not busy being a peace activist or a software developer, my favorite thing to do is sing opera. It’s been a thrill to me to sing ensemble with a couple of different community theater opera companies in New York City and Long Island. I’m a self-trained musician and hardly an exceptional singer, but I do always work hard in rehearsal and take my parts seriously, and that’s really what it takes to make community theater work.


Opera is only a recent obsession in my life, and what originally got me involved in opera is basically the same impulse that got me involved in peace activism: my desire to learn and understand world history. Reading a lot of books and trying to analyze and comprehend patterns in world history has been my lifelong pursuit and it has also been really my gateway to pacifism – and what I mean by this is that anybody who observes many historical and current wars and genocides and violent subjugations of peoples over the sweep of history will start to see a simple and obvious repeating pattern, which is that the decision to go to war is always a bad decision, rather like the decision of a habitual drunk driver to have a drink. Wars are sold as a method to solve conflicts, but this is a dangerously false promise, because in the real world wars never solve problems, but rather create new problems that lead to worse conflicts. Militarism also always leads to a degradation of government and a hollowing out of democracy, as war profiteers use their stolen gains to influence corrupt politicians to enable the continuance of their crimes.


The biggest pattern of all is that wars are self-replicators. A war may finally wrench to its painful end, when enough misery has been suffered on all sides, but time always reveals that wars of the past plant seeds for the wars of the future. No war ever really ends, and we can look at World War One, World War Two and today’s looming World War Three as evidence of this. It turns out that fear and racism and trauma from violence is passed down from generation to generation intact, with no reduction in intensity. These are the patterns I’ve learned from a lifelong study of world history.

title: "Catastrophe of Unimaginable Proportions": Nepal Flood Death Toll Tops 900; Near 5,000 Still Missing
content:
More than 900 people in Nepal are confirmed dead after a massive wall of water, mud and debris crashed through a Himalayan river valley on the border with Tibet. More than 4,200 people are missing in Nepal and hundreds more in Tibet. Families are searching hospitals for loved ones, and crews have buried hundreds of unidentified bodies in shallow graves. Rescue efforts are also underway for more than 900 hydropower workers, believed to be trapped in more than a dozen underground tunnels blocked by debris. The cause of the flash flooding is believed to have been the collapse of a glacier in the mountains, leading a wave of water, rocks and debris to carve its way through the valley.


“This is a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions,” says journalist Kunda Dixit, speaking to

Democracy Now!

 from the Nepalese capital of Kathmandu.


“We used to say that the glaciers are melting in the Himalaya. Now it seems like the mountains are cracking up,” says Dixit. “This has sort of redefined what global warming and climate change is doing, not just to Nepal and the Himalaya, but to the planet.”

title: Armed Israeli Settlers Kidnap British Activist
content:
Armed Israeli settlers kidnapped a British activist in the illegally occupied West Bank on Saturday, before locking him in a shed and then handing him over to police, his lawyer said. 


Finn Joughin, 22, was trying to prevent settlers from dismantling a fence in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair when two men dragged him away,

video of the incident

 shows. 


He was handed over to police but not charged with a crime, and was due to be deported on Sunday.   


“Without any hearing, the police have decided to move him to deportation, which just shows that this entire case has been political in the first place,” Joughin’s lawyer, Inbar Shaked Vard,

told the Associated Press

. “The only intention of police was to deport international activists who come to Israel in order to assist Palestinians.” 


She added: “He merely stood by the fence that the settlers were trying to dismantle, in order to prevent them from doing so. He was then kidnapped by armed men, who were not in uniform and therefore did not have authority to do so.”


The UK Foreign Office said it had raised the case with Israeli authorities. 


The incident happened amid a spike in violence by settlers and security forces against foreign observers in the West Bank over the weekend. 


Masked Israelis attacked three members of an NBC News crew as they interviewed a Palestinian woman in the town of Jalud on Saturday. Four men emerged from a car,

beat the crew and the woman

 with sticks and threw rocks at them, the outlet reported.  


Reporter Matt Bradley received treatment at a nearby clinic after being hit twice on the arm. The woman, 51-year-old Aida Ahmed Abdullah, received medical care from the Red Crescent. 


In Hebron,

video showed

 soldiers shouting and pointing their guns at unarmed Palestinians before shoving two journalists wearing press vests and ordering them to move back.


In the footage, journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy asks one of the soldiers: “Why did you just aim your rifle at children? You just aimed your rifle at a child.”

, including

, in

the West Bank since October 2023 as part of an intensifying campaign of ethnic cleansing that has largely been overshadowed by the genocide in Gaza.

title: Alemania: «la ridiculez de este juicio show»
content:
La argentina Leandra Rollo en el Tribunal Regional de Stuttgart. Foto: https://static.972mag.com


A casi un año del encarcelamiento de los Ulm 5,

continúa el juicio que fue prolongado hasta Enero de 2027

. Los llamados «Ulm5»: Zo, Crow, Vi, Leandra y Daniel irrumpieron el 8 de Septiembre del 2025 en una fábrica de la compańía de produccion de armas Israelí Elbit Systems, en la ciudad de Ulm.


Los Ulm 5 son activistas de Irlanda, Gran Bretaña, España, Argentina y Alemania que llevan años defendiendo los derechos de las y los palestinos por la vía legal, es decir, manifestaciones y peticiones a políticos, entre otras acciones. Su acción fue expresión de una profunda convicción: desobediencia civil dirigida exclusivamente contra bienes materiales con el fin de salvar vidas humanas.


Elbit Systems suministra el 86% de las armas al ejército israelí, con las mismas que se comete el Genocidio en Gaza contra el pueblo de Palestina y contra toda la humanidad.

 P

or Ana Muro, corresponsal de ANRed.


Ninguno de ellos tiene antecedentes penales. No perpetraron violencia contra ninguna persona, ni atemorizaron o amenazaron, siquiera anunciaron su acción, sino que la documentaron y se entregaron por propia voluntad a la Policía alemana.


Se les acusa de allanamiento y daños a la propiedad. Durante el proceso se discutía agregar otra acusación contra ellos e imputarles el delito de asociación ilícita, que implicaría una pena mayor.


Desde entonces, a pesar de no exteriorizar ninguna “peligrosidad” en la sociedad, y no dar indicios de peligro de fuga, los 5 están en prisión preventiva y repartidos por diferentes cárceles de maxima seguridad en el  Sur de Alemania, en condiciones de detención extremadamente duras. Éstas, afortunadamente, se van flexibilizando paulatinamente, gracias a los reclamos de abogados, grupos defensores de Derechos Humanos, familiares, camaradas y amigas.


En el juicio, se pueden visibilizar innumerables irregularidades cometidas por el Tribunal Regional de Stuttgart, en detrimentos de los derechos y garantías procesales de las y los acusados.

 


La defensa alegó que el acto imputado está amparado por la legítima defensa frente a un genocidio y rechazó enérgicamente la acusación de antisemitismo. El Tribunal Regional de Stuttgart casi triplicó la duración del juicio, fijando 28 fechas adicionales, a las 16 vistas anunciadas inicialmente. Esto prolonga el calvario hasta enero de 2027, es decir, ocho meses y medio, algo totalmente desproporcionado. El Tribunal está violando el principio de celeridad, que debe tenerse especialmente en cuenta en este caso de prisión preventiva.


A pesar de las peticiones de la defensa, se negó a investigar el papel de Elbit Systems Deutschland en el genocidio de Gaza y demás crímenes de guerra perpetrados por el Ejército israelí. Sin embargo la Defensa insiste en este punto central. La defensa ha solicitado que se interrogue al director general de Elbit Systems Deutschland, el señor Rachow, como testigo para que confirme los crímenes de guerra cometidos en Gaza. La defensa está convencida de que Elbit Systems Deutschland GmbH und Co. KG forma parte integrante de las operaciones bélicas en Gaza. Afirman que está  integrada en el grupo empresarial Elbit Systems, mediante una división del trabajo, y apoya las operaciones bélicas del ejército israelí en Gaza, en particular mediante la transferencia de tecnología, el suministro de material de defensa y componentes a Israel, y vínculos financieros. El tribunal aún no se ha pronunciado sobre la solicitud de pruebas.


Entre los 5, una argentina


Leandra nació en Argentina, en la ciudad de Quilmes.


En una de las intervenciones que Leandra pudo realizar,

en el contexto del juicio, expresó entre otras ideas y pronunciamientos

: 


“Detener el genocidio no es, principalmente, una exigencia política, sino ética. Porque, cuando la maquinaria del poder opresor se dirige contra quienes menos poder tienen, existe el deber ético de detenerla por todos los medios necesarios”. 


“En diciembre de 2024, un informe de Amnistía Internacional concluyó que la «escala y magnitud sin precedentes» del ataque israelí contra Gaza constituye un genocidio. „

Eine Mehrheit der Deutschen lehnt die Reformen des Sozialsystems ab. Die Ablehnung reicht einer Umfrage zufolge über fast alle Parteigrenzen hinweg. Besonders junge Menschen sind stark verunsichert.


Die laufenden Debatten über Reformen des Sozialsystems führen zu einer massiven Verunsicherung in der Bevölkerung. Laut einer am Freitag veröffentlichten Studie des Instituts für Makroökonomie und Konjunkturforschung (IMK) der gewerkschaftsnahen Hans-Böckler-Stiftung sorgen sich 81 Prozent der erwachsenen Deutschen um ihre soziale Absicherung. 42 Prozent der Menschen schränken demnach deswegen ihren privaten Konsum ein, was die Binnennachfrage schwäche.


Die Studie beruht auf einer repräsentativen Online-Befragung von rund 4000 Menschen in Deutschland im Alter von 18 bis 75 Jahren im Zeitraum vom 17. Juni bis 13. Juli. Aus der Umfrage geht laut IMK auch hervor, dass 76 Prozent der Befragten die geplanten oder teilweise schon beschlossenen Maßnahmen ablehnen. 55 Prozent äußerten sich sogar stark ablehnend

…“

(…) Neben Siemens befinden sich unter den Unterzeichnenden des Briefs einige Vertreter:innen der Automobilbranche mit Unternehmen wie Audi, BMW, Porsche sowie dem Zulieferer ZF. Darüber hinaus sind es aber auch Konzerne wie Siemens und die Spitzen der Metall-Kapitalverbände von Baden-Württemberg und Bayern. Dass die Automobilbranche an den Reformen ein besonders großes Interesse hat, wundert nicht. Immerhin wird sie nicht müde zu erzählen, wie schwer sie es gerade hat, und droht dabei auch mit Massenentlassungen und Werksschließungen. (…) Dass die Automobilbranche weniger Gewinn macht als noch letztes Jahr oder vor ein paar Jahren, stimmt (…). Trotzdem werden immer noch regelmäßig Milliardengewinne eingefahren: So erzielte BMW im ersten Halbjahr 2026 zum Beispiel immer noch einen Nettogewinn von 2,87 Milliarden Euro. Das sind zwar 28,5 Prozent weniger als im Vorjahr, ist jedoch trotzdem eine riesige Summe an Geld. VW und Porsche machten sogar mit 5,9 Milliarden und 1,35 Milliarden Euro gar keinen Verlust, konnten aber ihren Gewinn auch nicht groß steigern. Die Krise der Automobilbranche besteht also (noch) nicht darin, gar nicht mehr profitabel oder existenzfähig zu sein, sondern nur darin, dass ihr Profit den Konzernchefs nicht genügt. Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) encompasses human rights relating to sexuality, reproductive health, and bodily autonomy. In this episode, our guest outlines the core components of SRHR span universal health coverage, personal freedoms, and global development frameworks. Michelle Oyuga, a human rights lawyer and gender justice advocate, talks to The Elephant.


The post

author: Wandia Njoya
title: Strange Bedfellows: What’s Faith Got to Do With Identity
content:
What does faith have to do with identity? This is what I asked when I was invited to give a keynote lecture on 18 September 2025 at a workshop held at the Centre for Interfaith Studies in Africa at the Hekima University College in Nairobi. The theme of the workshop was “Law, Education and Interfaith Relations in Kenya”.


I will again begin my reflections with this question: What does faith have to do with identity? My answer today, although I might change my mind later on, is going to be provocative. I think faith has nothing to do with identity. In my presentation, I argue that if we are truly people of faith, the question of identity should not be anywhere near our faith. And I will anchor my argument in the stories of healing in the gospels.


​When I received the invitation to give the lecture, the first story I thought of was that of Jesus with the Samaritan woman at the well, narrated in John 4. 


The passage reveals an extended discussion of identity, in the worldly sense of identity as we know it today. We know identity as exclusion, boundaries, and conflict, rather than as unity, love, and sharing. But remember the political regime of the time of Jesus was the Roman Empire, which the British Empire mimicked when they came here in the late 1800s, and then left another mimicry called independence. We are therefore living under a mimicry of the same Roman Empire under which Jesus lived. 


The political logic that runs the Euro-American global empire, now in decline, was revived in Europe in the 17

th

 century from the ruins of the Roman Empire in a process that was baptized the Renaissance. As far as I’m concerned, there was no renaissance. It was a festival of exploring and excavating graves, in the same way the colonialists did when they came to Africa in the early 1900s, and still do, in the name of verifying whether we were “civilized”. The Roman Empire died in 476 of the Common Era, but when the wealthy of Europe, like the Medici family, wanted to impress the rest of Italy and Europe, they hired artists and scientists to excavate the graves and monuments of the dead empire and seek inspiration for something new. They essentially looked for the living among the dead. So, ideas such as the state, senate, law, and even the management of people of multiple cultural backgrounds, were borrowed from the ruins of Rome.  


Rome operated as a centralized government with a multicultural mix of people from the peripheral provinces of the empire. Not all people of the empire were considered Romans or citizens. Historians mark the reign of Augustus as the point at which citizenship transformed from being an active one about rights and duties, to a passive one about legal status and honour. Under Augustus, the Latin language gained more prominence as a marker of “Romanness”, and the empire continued to make a distinction between those who were born in Rome and those who were not. Later on, as Rome began to decline, it invited the Barbarians, whom they considered the Germanic peoples to be, to fight for the Roman empire while simultaneously not accessing the rights of citizens of Rome.


The Romans named “Barbarians” those whom they considered to be outsiders to the empire, those whose languages were incomprehensible to them.

While Western epistemology has since clarified that the Germanic, Slavic, Croat, Turkish, and other Europeans were those to whom the Romans attached the tag “Barbarian”, it has not done equal favour to North Africa, where “Berbers” and “Arabs” are still ethnically tied to the imperial term. Meanwhile, the expression “barbarians at the gate” became a popular one to capture the fear of the insiders that their city was facing imminent collapse at the hands of immigrants.


Back to John 4. As we see in his conversation with the Samaritan woman, Jesus, who had lived in that same Roman Empire, rejected this imperial view of identity, where discrimination is unspoken yet real when it comes to human interactions. When he asks for water, he’s speaking as one human being to another. But what does the Samaritan woman say? To paraphrase her, she says: “According to my ethnicity, I’m not worthy to give you water.” Then Jesus replies, “But the water I’m providing is of eternal life, meaning that even when I ask you for literal water, I reject this imperial idea of human hierarchy.”


Then Jesus tests her with another identity, which is that of gender. He asks her for a husband, and then reveals that he …

author: Duda Sousa
title: Fim da Escala 6×1 será votado no Senado em esforço concentrado antes do recesso eleitoral
content:
O último esforço concentrado do Congresso Nacional para votações antes das eleições termina nesta semana. A principal disputa deve ficar em torno do fim da escala 6×1. Na quarta-feira, a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado deve analisar a Proposta de Emenda Constitucional (PEC) que reduz a jornada semanal de 44 para 40 horas e garante dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana, sem redução salarial. O relator, senador Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), apresentou na última quinta-feira (27) parecer favorável à manutenção do texto aprovado pela Câmara dos Deputados e rejeitou as 12 emendas apresentadas por outros senadores. Se passar pela CCJ, a PEC ainda precisará ser votada em dois turnos no plenário do Senado.


Também deve ser analisado pelo Senado nesta semana o PL 2.780/2024, sob relatoria do Senador Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), que cria a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos. O tema ganhou peso diante do interesse estrangeiro pelas reservas brasileiras de terras raras e da preocupação em manter no país as etapas de maior valor agregado da cadeia produtiva. A proposta busca estimular a pesquisa, extração, beneficiamento e transformação desses minerais, importantes para setores como transição energética, tecnologia e defesa.


Também está no radar do Congresso a Medida Provisória (MP) 1.357/2026, que suspende temporariamente a cobrança do Imposto de Importação sobre compras internacionais de até 50 dólares, a chamada “taxa das blusinhas”. A medida perde a validade em 8 de setembro, e o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), pretende levar o texto rapidamente aos plenários das duas Casas.


Corrida Eleitoral


A próxima semana será a primeira com exibição todos os dias do horário eleitoral gratuito no rádio e na televisão. A propaganda começou na última sexta-feira (28) e seguirá até 1º de outubro, com programas para presidente às terças, quintas e sábados e inserções ao longo da programação. Além disso, a disputa presidencial também terá uma rodada de sabatinas da Jovem Pan.


A programação começa nesta segunda-feira, 31 de agosto, com Ronaldo Caiado (PSD). A terça será o dia de Renan Santos (Missão), e a quarta-feira terá o presidente Lula (PT). Na quinta-feira, 3 de setembro, a emissora recebe Romeu Zema (Novo) e fecha a programação com o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), na sexta. As entrevistas serão exibidas sempre das 8h às 9h, durante o Jornal da Manhã.


STF e PF: encontro busca reduzir as divergências


Enquanto as campanhas avançam por todo o Brasil, o governo também tenta reduzir uma tensão entre a Polícia Federal (PF) e o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). O diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Rodrigues, deve se reunir nesta semana com o ministro André Mendonça. O encontro foi articulado pelo presidente Lula e deverá ser mediado pelo ministro da Justiça, Wellington César Lima e Silva, com possível participação do advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias. A conversa ocorre em meio às divergências sobre investigações conduzidas pela PF e decisões do ministro em casos de forte repercussão política. Entre eles, as apurações sobre o Banco Master, as fraudes no INSS e as investigações envolvendo o filho do presidente, Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, o Lulinha.


Estão na agenda da semana de 31 de agosto a 4 de setembro:


TSE:


Consulta à seção eleitoral (1/9):

 A partir desta terça-feira (1º), eleitores poderão consultar, pelo e-Título ou pela internet, a seção onde irão votar, já com informações sobre eventuais transferências temporárias de local de votação. A data é diferente do que havia sido indicado anteriormente: o calendário oficial do TSE estabelece o dia 1º de setembro. 


DIREITOS HUMANOS


Câmara


Maioridade penal (Comissão Especial da PEC 32/2015, 1/9, 14h):

 Comissão especial analisa requerimentos para realização de audiência pública sobre a redução da maioridade penal. O debate deve abordar se a idade penal é protegida como cláusula pétrea da Constituição e os limites para alterar direitos e garantias individuais previstos na Carta de 1988.


Publicidade de bets nas redes sociais (CEXBRLEG, 1/9, 15h):

 Audiência discute os impactos da publicidade de apostas online e de jogos de azar, como o “tigrinho”, nas redes sociais e nas grandes plataformas de tecnologia. A audiência deve abordar também o papel das chamadas big techs no combate à pirataria e na circulação de publicidade do mercado de apostas.

author: Alice Maciel
title: Mansões, carros de luxo, viagens: a vida de Eduardo Bolsonaro e Figueiredo nos EUA
content:
Mansões, carros de luxo, viagens, restaurantes caros. Enquanto fazem lobby para tentar enfraquecer o governo brasileiro e o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) junto ao governo de Donald Trump, o ex-deputado federal Eduardo Bolsonaro e o influenciador Paulo Figueiredo mantêm um alto padrão de vida nos Estados Unidos (EUA).


Ambos já afirmaram enfrentar dificuldades financeiras devido ao que chamam de “perseguição política”. No entanto, um levantamento da

Agência Pública

 e do

ICL Notícias

 revela um cenário diferente. Além de viverem em casas milionárias, no último ano os dois adquiriram carros caros, têm frequentado restaurantes sofisticados, mantêm os filhos em escolas particulares e acumularam uma extensa agenda de viagens.


Eduardo Bolsonaro e Paulo Figueiredo foram centrais na articulação para impor tarifas contra o Brasil e retaliações contra ministros do Supremo. Desde 2025, eles participaram de dezenas de reuniões com deputados republicanos e membros do governo dos EUA pedindo intervenções em resposta à condenação do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro por tentativa de golpe de Estado em 8 de janeiro de 2023.


Em maio de 2025, três meses após se mudar para o Texas e anunciar que viveria uma espécie de “autoexílio”, Eduardo Bolsonaro comprou um carro novo. Não exatamente um modelo econômico para atravessar tempos difíceis. Ele adquiriu um GMC Acadia Elevation 2025 preto, um SUV de três fileiras de assentos, avaliado em cerca de 43,8 mil dólares nos EUA, o que equivale a aproximadamente R$ 226 mil.


Os registros de gastos associados à família Bolsonaro nos EUA mostram que, desde a mudança para o país, em fevereiro do ano passado, o padrão de vida não parece ter encolhido, nem mesmo após o STF determinar o bloqueio dos bens de Eduardo Bolsonaro e de sua esposa, Heloísa Bolsonaro, em julho de 2025. Eduardo ainda perdeu o salário que recebia como deputado federal em dezembro, quando seu mandato foi cassado por faltas, e, desde 2015, não recebe salário como escrivão da PF, de onde a corporação

recomendou

 sua demissão por abandono do cargo.


Ao chegar aos EUA, o ex-deputado escolheu Arlington, no Texas, onde já havia mantido uma empresa entre 2023 e 2024. A residência alugada estava longe de ter as dimensões de um refúgio improvisado. Tinha pouco mais de 300 metros quadrados, quatro quartos e quatro banheiros, com valor de mercado estimado em 707,7 mil dólares (cerca de R$ 3,6 milhões). O valor da locação anunciado em sites imobiliários, quando eles alugaram a casa, era de 4,5 mil dólares,  aproximadamente R$ 23,3 mil na cotação atual.


Em maio de 2025, Jair Bolsonaro chegou a

transferir

 R$ 2 milhões ao filho. “Botei dinheiro na mão dele, dinheiro limpo, legal, Pix”,

afirmou

 o ex-presidente.


Dias depois, Eduardo chegou a reclamar para o pai, em mensagens trocadas por Whatsapp, que estava “se fodendo” nos EUA. Ao reclamar de uma entrevista em que Jair dizia que o filho era imaturo, Eduardo reclamou que, ao jogar ele para baixo, o ex-presidente o estaria condenando a passar o “resto da vida nessa porra aqui”. “VTNC seu ingrato do caralho!”, escreveu.


A situação parece ter melhorado desde então. Pouco mais de um ano depois, em maio de 2026, a família trocou Arlington por um endereço ainda mais valorizado, em Southlake, uma das cidades mais ricas do Texas, onde a renda familiar média é de 250 mil dólares – três vezes maior do que em Arlington, por exemplo. Eduardo, a esposa e os dois filhos moram atualmente em uma casa que oferece “uma vida de resort”, conforme

revelou

 o

The Intercept Brasil

.


Avaliada em 1,22 milhão de dólares, cerca de R$ 6 milhões, a mansão foi anunciada para aluguel por aproximadamente 5,9 mil dólares (em torno de R$ 30 mil mensais), segundo anúncios imobiliários que permaneceram ativos até fevereiro deste ano. O imóvel tem 424 metros quadrados de área construída, em um terreno de 1.366 metros quadrados, quatro quartos e piscina, além de acesso a um clube com quadras de tênis e a uma lagoa.


A filha mais velha do casal Bolsonaro, de cinco anos, foi matriculada numa escola cristã a cerca de 15 minutos de casa, com custo anual de 18 mil dólares (R$ 93,4 mil), conforme divulgado no site da escola.


Eduardo nega ter usado parte da verba do filme Dark Horse para custear sua vida nos EUA. O filme foi financiado com cerca de R$ 61 milhões do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, por meio do Fundo Havengate. O negócio veio à tona após reportagem do

title: Örhan: All institutions must unite against drug addiction
content:
Concerns over drug use and substance addiction are growing in the Sur district of Diyarbakır (Amed). Children and young people in particular are increasingly being targeted by drug networks, prompting public concern as drug use becomes more visible across neighbourhoods.


Research conducted across the city, along with accounts from healthcare workers, indicates that the age at which children are first exposed to substance use has fallen to increasingly younger ages. There are growing calls for comprehensive public and preventive policies to curb drug use in the district and protect young people.


Sur Municipality Co-Mayor Adnan Örhan spoke to ANF about drug use and addiction in the district.


An open wound in society


Örhan said substance addiction had become one of society’s “open wounds,” adding that since taking office, the municipality had identified the drawing of children and young people into networks of addiction as one of the most serious problems facing the district. 


He said: “Since we took office more than two and a half years ago, one of the most serious problems we have observed and witnessed in society is, unfortunately, young people and children being lured into the trap of substance addiction. There are underlying reasons for this. It is not something that emerged on its own. After trustees were appointed in 2016, virtually all public spaces were shut down. Society as a whole was effectively denied room to breathe.


When spaces for children, women and young people were completely closed down, and society was suffocated under an oppressive form of governance, unfortunately, some malicious gangs, groups and individuals sought to draw young people and children into drug networks.”


 


Families cannot go out in the evenings


Örhan said substance addiction could not be treated solely as a health issue and stressed the importance of properly lighting the streets of Sur and making them safer. 


Örhan said: “When we go out into the streets, we are confronted with the cries of families. Mothers, women and children tell us about this time and again. They say, ‘We cannot go out into the streets after a certain hour in the evening.’ In Sur in particular, the situation has become extremely serious.


For nearly two years, we have held talks with Dicle Electricity Distribution Company (DEDAŞ) over street lighting in Sur. We raised the issue at a meeting attended by officials from the governor’s office and DEDAŞ, but they told us that the problem had still not been resolved. Street lighting is of vital importance for Sur.


Families, women and children who cannot go outside after dark are unfortunately forced to leave the streets to people using drugs. Extremely disturbing incidents are taking place here. We see that this, in turn, brings prostitution, harassment and rape, as well as the proliferation of gangs.”


Substance addiction, gangs and poverty are interconnected


Örhan said that tackling only the consequences of substance addiction would not be enough. He said: “When you suffocate a society and deny it social and economic opportunities, people with malicious intentions find many ways and methods to deceive young people and children and draw them into these networks. Unfortunately, this has become much more prevalent in poorer neighbourhoods.


Drug networks are able to operate more freely, particularly in neighbourhoods facing economic hardship. You can see this with your own eyes. To prevent the problem from worsening, the central government needs to develop social and economic policies.”


We are working to free Amed from substance addiction


Örhan said that local administrations were carrying out a range of initiatives to combat addiction, adding that, together with the work of the Şiyar Be Platform over the past year, they were pursuing a collective effort to prevent addiction in Diyarbakır.


Örhan also said: “We are carrying out serious efforts to free Amed from substance addiction as much as possible and to protect our young people from it. Rehabilitation centers have been opened, as well as counseling centers for substance addiction. We have colleagues working in these centers. Public meetings are held at certain times. We are working to raise awareness among people and encourage them to support these efforts. We believe that we will make significant progress in this regard.”


Gang activity threatens public safety

title: Başaran'a, Gökay'a özgürlük
content:
Onlar,


Epeydir unutulmuş bir sendikacılık pratiğini yeniden hatırlattılar.


Makam odalarından değil; işçilerin arasında, sokakta, yolda, parkta, meydanda ısrarla, pes etmeden sendikacılık yaptılar.


Sahici.


Güven verici.


Kararlı.


Hak arayan işçilerle yan yana, omuz omuza, geceler ve günler boyunca, güneşin ve yağmurun altında oldular.


İşçinin sesinin duyulmadığı yerde ses oldular.


Görülmeyen mücadeleyi görünür kıldılar.


Yeri geldi, ülke gündemini belirlediler.


Direndiler.


Kazandılar.


Kimi zaman verilen sözler tutulmadığında yeniden düştüler yollara.


Başaran Aksu ve Gökay Çakır, işçilerin hakları için mücadele ederken sayısız kez gözaltına alındılar. Her gözaltı sonrasında geri çekilmediler, “Yorulduk.” demediler.


Kaldıkları yerden yeniden başladılar.


Yılmadılar.


Pes etmediler.


Vazgeçmediler.


Çünkü onların sendikacılık anlayışında mücadele, bir meslek ya da bir iş değildi. İşçinin ekmeği, onuru ve geleceği için verilmesi gereken soylu bir kavgaydı.


Koca koca sendikaların sustuğu, mücadele etmek yerine yasak savma anlayışıyla hareket ettiği zamanlarda onlar, işçilerin kavgasını büyüttüler.


Defalarca Ankara yollarına düştüler.


Parklarda sabahladılar.


Geceleri işçilerle birlikte geçirdiler.


Gündüzleri yine işçilerin yanında oldular.


Bazen bir pankartın arkasında, bazen bir fabrikanın önünde, bazen bir yol kenarında…


Bazen sarı baretlerini vura vura haklarını istediler.


Şimdi yüksek sesle sormalıyız:


Sendikacılık yapmak, hak aramak, bunda ısrar etmek suç mu?


İşçilerin taleplerini dile getirmek suç mu?


Onlar her defasında madencilerin yanında durdular.


Haklarını isteyen emekçilerle birlikte yürüdüler.


Taleplerini duyurmaya çalıştılar.


Sendikacının görevi, işçiyi, emekçiyi savunmak değil midir zaten. 


Onlar kolayı seçmediler.


Baskılara boyun eğmediler.


Geri adım atmadılar. Kararları, direnen işçilerle birlikte aldılar.


Verdikleri sözleri tuttular.


Bu nedenle onların mücadelesi yalnızca iki kişinin hikâyesinden ibaret değildir.


Bugün onları tutuklayarak mücadele alanından uzaklaştırabileceklerini düşünenler, belki de en önemli şeyi gözden kaçırıyorlar:


Mücadele, yalnızca mücadele edenlerden ibaret değildir.


Onlarla birlikte yürüyen, direnen madenciler vefalıdır.


Onlardan cesaret alan emekçiler yaşadıklarını unutmaz.


Buzu kıranların, yolu açanların ardından yürüyenler mutlaka çıkacaktır.


Ve mücadelenin seyir defteri, yolu açanları unutmaz.


Tarih de unutmaz. Ötesi gururla not eder.


Bugün Başaran Aksu ve Gökay Çakır dört duvar arasında olabilir.


Ama onların mücadelesi dört duvar arasına sığmaz.


Tam da bu nedenle bugün yapılması gereken, Başaran ve Gökay’ın mücadelesini daha fazla sahiplenmektir.


İşçilerin, emekçilerin, sendikacıların hak arama mücadelesini kriminalize etmeye çalışanlara inat, onların yanında daha güçlü durmalıyız.


Çünkü bugün mesele yalnızca Başaran ve Gökay değildir.


İşçinin örgütlenme hakkıdır.


Mesele, hak aramanın suç olmadığıdır.


Mesele, emeğin ve alın terinin değersizleştirilmesine karşı söz söyleyebilmektir.


Ve yarın başka işçiler, başka emekçiler haklarını aradığında, “Başaran ve Gökay gibi sendikacılar da var.” denilmesidir. 


Başaran’ın özgürlüğü, Gökay’ın özgürlüğü yalnızca onların özgürlüğü değildir.


Bu, işçinin mücadele hakkının özgürlüğüdür.


Bu, sendikacılığın özgürlüğüdür.


Bu, hak arama iradesinin özgürlüğüdür.


O yüzden bugün daha yüksek sesle söylemeliyiz:


BAŞARAN’A ÖZGÜRLÜK!


GÖKAY’A ÖZGÜRLÜK!


(RU/Mİ)

author: Brian Hioe
title: Central Election Commission Rejects Caning, Traffic Fine Referendum, Approves Nuclear Referendum
content:
THE CENTRAL ELECTION COMMISSION (CEC) has rejected two out of the three referendums advanced by the pan-Blue camp.

The KMT’s proposed referendum on caning for offenses such as sexual assault, large-scale fraud, and child abuse was thrown out. Likewise, so, too, was a referendum question proposed by the TPP that would have allocated fines from traffic violations to local governments for improving traffic safety.

The CEC was more divided on the issue of traffic violations, voting 4-3 against the proposal. By contrast, the CEC voted unanimously against the caning proposal. The justification for preventing the two referendums was that they did not fall under the purview of what referendums should cover.

Human rights groups have largely hailed the rejection of the caning proposal. The proposal would have contravened international human rights conventions that Taiwan has voluntarily ratified and would have likely drawn international exposure in such a way as to make Taiwan a laughingstock. It is largely countries that are former British colonies or which have Sharia law that have caning as a punishment.

To this extent, there was no widespread social demand for caning before the KMT made the proposal. The KMT itself appeared internally divided on the issue, with KMT chair Cheng Li-wun wanting to back down from the issue before apparent resistance from the KMT legislative caucus.

As for traffic violations, one can situate this referendum question in line with continued budgetary contention between local and central governments. The TPP, however, had not previously leaned particularly strongly into the issue of traffic safety, making it very possible that it proposed the question in order to have a political agenda distinctive from that of the KMT when it came to elections.

So, then, the only referendum question approved by the CEC will be on nuclear energy. The referendum question will be to call for the abolition of policies that mandate the establishment of a nuclear-free homeland. In this sense, the KMT would be attempting to leverage on a platform traditionally popular with its base.

And yet one notes that there have been four referendum questions pushed for by the pan-Blue camp on nuclear energy in the last decade. There is little that is distinctive about once again calling for an end to policies for a nuclear-free homeland and, this time around, the KMT did not campaign with the public to hold a referendum but instead pushed through a referendum using its current control of the Legislative Yuan.

Likewise, President Lai Ching-te has already reversed course on the DPP’s historic opposition to nuclear energy to submit plans for the restarts of two reactors. This reversal was in order to placate international concerns about nuclear energy as facilitating Taiwan’s current AI boom, as well as the energy demands that would have to be met in the event of an invasion. But even as the DPP claims that it still has the long-term aim of a nuclear-free homeland, this reversal may ultimately take the winds out of the KMT’s sails.

More generally, the KMT did not actually have to put the issues that it proposed for national referendums to a vote; it could have simply used its current control over the legislature to push them through into law. As such, its referendum aims this time are quite clear in order to influence elections. Yet one notes that the CEC’s rejection of referendum questions shows that Michael You’s CEC can be combative when it comes to throwing out what is allowed to be put to the national referendum, this despite the fact that–as former head of the Taiwan Public Opinion Foundation–You appears to have originally been put in his position as an olive branch to the KMT.
